sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

Marrowford sits where the slow brown Marrow River bends under a stone bridge, a town of grain barges, tallow-chandlers and market stalls that never quite close. The lands around it are old and quarrelsome. Minor noble houses hold the river-farms, trade in favours, and pay well for stories that make their lineages look older than they are.

Wren Ashgrove is nineteen, half-elf, a bard with a quick grin and a sharper tongue. She was raised by Corvin Tallowmere, who taught her to spin tales and sell them. A few weeks ago she slipped away from his caravan at a river crossing in the night. She took his ledger of forged tales, its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter, a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She also carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, the gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers, with a curl of old parchment inside that may be a true blessing or just another forgery.

Dusk settles over Marrowford's square. Lamps are being lit along the stalls, and the smell of river fish and woodsmoke hangs in the air. At the square's far edge, half in shadow, stands a wagon painted with a shrine-lantern sigil you know too well. Corvin's. There's no sign of the man himself.

A weathered driver lounges on the box, picking his teeth. Before him a young page in a minor noble's livery, pale and sweating, is pressing a sealed letter into his hand and glancing over his shoulder. The wax seal is one you've seen in the ledger. On the tailboard behind them sits a locked, iron-bound strongbox, begging to be poked at.

The crowd is thin enough that you could slip closer unseen, march up with a grin, or wait and watch. What does Wren do?

I keep to the shadow of a grain-stall and slip closer, trying to stay unseen and get near enough to hear what the page says to the driver. While I'm at it, I pull out my road-psalter and flip to the margin notes to check whose seal that is in the ledger.

Dexterity measures agility, reflexes, and balance.

#### Dexterity Checks

A Dexterity check can model any attempt to move nimbly, quickly, or quietly, or to keep from falling on tricky footing. The Acrobatics, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Dexterity checks.

***Acrobatics.*** Your Dexterity (Acrobatics) check covers your attempt to stay on your feet in a tricky situation, such as when you're trying to run across a sheet of ice, balance on a tightrope, or stay upright on a rocking ship's deck. The GM might also call for a Dexterity (Acrobatics) check to see if you can perform acrobatic stunts, including dives, rolls, somersaults, and flips.

***Sleight of Hand.*** Whenever you attempt an act of legerdemain or manual trickery, such as planting something on someone else or concealing an object on your person, make a Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check. The GM might also call for a Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check to determine whether you can lift a coin purse off another person or slip something out of another person's pocket.

***Stealth.*** Make a Dexterity (Stealth) check when you attempt to conceal yourself from enemies, slink past guards, slip away without being noticed, or sneak up on someone without being seen or heard.

***Other Dexterity Checks.*** The GM might call for a Dexterity check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:
- Control a heavily laden cart on a steep descent
- Steer a chariot around a tight turn
- Pick a lock
- Disable a trap
- Securely tie up a prisoner
- Wriggle free of bonds

- Craft a small or detailed object

#### Attack Rolls and Damage

You add your Dexterity modifier to your attack roll and your damage roll when attacking with a ranged weapon, such as a sling or a longbow. You can also add your Dexterity modifier to your attack roll and your damage roll when attacking with a melee weapon that has the finesse property, such as a dagger or a rapier.

#### Armor Class

Depending on the armor you wear, you might add some or all of your Dexterity modifier to your Armor Class.

#### Initiative

At the beginning of every combat, you roll initiative by making a Dexterity check. Initiative determines the order of creatures' turns in combat.

#### Hiding

The GM decides when circumstances are appropriate for hiding. When you try to hide, make a Dexterity (Stealth) check. Until you are discovered or you stop hiding, that check's total is contested by the Wisdom (Perception) check of any creature that actively searches for signs of your presence.

You can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, and you give away your position if you make noise, such as shouting a warning or knocking over a vase.

An invisible creature can always try to hide. Signs of its passage might still be noticed, and it does have to stay quiet.

In combat, most creatures stay alert for signs of danger all around, so if you come out of hiding and approach a creature, it usually sees you. However, under certain circumstances, the GM might allow you to stay hidden as you approach a creature that is distracted, allowing you to gain advantage on an attack roll before you are seen.

***Passive Perception.*** When you hide, there's a chance someone will notice you even if they aren't searching. To determine whether such a creature notices you, the GM compares your Dexterity (Stealth) check with that creature's passive Wisdom (Perception) score, which equals 10 + the creature's Wisdom modifier, as well as any other bonuses or penalties. If the creature has advantage, add 5. For disadvantage, subtract 5. For example, if a 1st-level character (with a proficiency bonus of +2) has a Wisdom of 15 (a +2 modifier) and proficiency in Perception, he or she has a passive Wisdom (Perception) of 14.

***What Can You See?*** One of the main factors in determining whether you can find a hidden creature or object is how well you can see in an area, which might be **lightly** or **heavily obscured**, as explained in chapter 8, "Adventuring."

Your Investigation check was a 19. You lift the canvas flap and slip inside the cramped wagon. Under the smell of lamp oil and old wool, your trained eye finds what a casual one wouldn't.

A small folding travelling shrine of the Lantern-Bearer stands against the front panel. Its back panel sits a hair proud of the frame, and behind it is a flat leather case. Inside are sheets of blank vellum, a tin of wax-impressions, a Verrel seal among them, and a half-finished draft in Corvin's neat, unmistakable hand. It reads: *"...to be mended before the assessor arrives. The Verrel charter's third descent must hold, or the ink on the whole line will not."* Beneath it is a list of three noble houses with sums beside them, two struck through and one circled: Verrel.

So Corvin is fixing his own forgery, and he knows it's about to be exposed. There's no second ledger and no satchel, only a cot, a cloak, and the case. You could take the draft, copy it, or leave it as you found it. The sealing-wax impressions would be useful to a forger.

Outside, the tavern door bangs. The driver hasn't come back yet, but a minute or two is all you have. The page is still on the far side of the bridge, getting smaller.

What does Wren do with the case, and then do you still tail the page?

I snatch the wax-impression tin and quickly copy the draft's key lines onto a sheet of my own paper with my pen, then slip the original back behind the shrine panel exactly as I found it so Corvin never knows. Then I slide out the back of the wagon, keep to the shadows, and tail the page across the bridge.

You buckle the rapier back on. Tobin watches you do it, then chews his lip, thinking hard in the way of someone who has never been asked a question like this.

"The charter's in an iron chest in my lord's study, at Thornhallow, under the window. The key's on a chain around his neck. But Hale has a copy; I've seen him use it when my lord's asleep." He swallows. "As for trust... my lord doesn't trust strangers. He doesn't trust anyone but Master Tallowmere, and he's frightened because Master Tallowmere hasn't answered him in a month."

He glances at your lute, and something stirs in his face. "There was a girl once. Years back, before I served there. The old cook still tells it. A storyteller came to Thornhallow with a girl who sang at my lord's table, and my lord wept at the last verse and gave her a ribbon. Was that... you?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. "If you came to my lord as the storyteller's apprentice, with a word or a token only that circle would know, he might listen. Thornhallow's a day's walk downriver, and the assessor comes in three days. I leave at dawn on a hired mule. I could say nothing of you, or I could say a friend of Master Tallowmere is coming."

The night is quiet, and the market lamps are going out one by one behind you. You hold a copy of Corvin's draft, a tin of his seal impressions, and a ledger of his lies in your psalter binding. Whatever you choose to do about Verrel's third descent, you can do it with all of them.

The market is just waking, with stalls unshuttering and the smell of hot dough in the cold air. A tinker with a tray of picks, files and tiny mirrors has a proper set of thieves' tools, but he wants 25 gp for it, and you have under fifteen. You could haggle some other day. Instead you spend 1 sp 2 cp on a loaf and a hunk of cheese, and that's your breakfast and lunch.

The river road runs down the Marrow's north bank through willow-banks, wheat fields gone gold, and stone farmsteads with smoke rising. You keep your eyes on the road, on every cart, every tradesman, every man whose smile lingers a beat too long. You see nothing. For a moment you wonder whether that's good luck or just poor looking, and you can't be sure which. Your Perception check was a natural 1, and nothing you saw tells you either way.

You walk through the day with your lute on your back, stopping to eat on a milestone and refill your waterskin at a roadside trough. The sun is slanting low when the road tops a rise and the land opens out. Below sits Thornhallow: a small walled manor on a bend of the river, grey stone with a slate roof, a gatehouse flying a green and white pennant, and a village of thatched cottages leaning against its wall like children against a parent. Smoke curls from the chimneys. It is a quarter past three.

There's a guard at the gate, and the manor is quiet. Somewhere inside, Tobin has arrived, and a worried lord is waiting for a friend of Corvin Tallowmere.

I smooth my cloak, put on a calm, slightly weary smile, and walk up to the gate guard. "Good afternoon. I'm a friend of Master Corvin Tallowmere, come at Lord Edric's request; Tobin should have said I was on the road. Your Persuasion check was a 13, enough. The guard is a stout, grey-whiskered man in a green tabard. He hears you through, chews on the word "ribbon," and his face changes. "Wait here," he says, and he sends a boy running across the yard.

It's a plain room, stone-walled, with a lit fire despite the warm day and a heavy desk covered in unsealed papers. Under the window sits an iron-bound chest, just as Tobin said.

Lord Edric Verrel stands when you enter. He is a narrow, stooped man of perhaps fifty, with ink on his cuffs and shadows under his eyes. Tobin hovers at his shoulder, pale and watching you.

"I was told a friend of Master Tallowmere was coming," Lord Edric says. His voice is thin and careful. "Tobin tells me you remember a ribbon. Many people could have learned that from a servant's gossip. Show me, if you would, what you have."

Beside the desk, in a shadowed corner, a man you haven't seen before sits quietly with a ledger open on his knee. He is neat, middle-aged and softly spoken, and he gives you a courteous, perfectly warm smile. He hasn't been introduced.

I keep my eyes on Lord Edric and ignore the smiling man in the corner. I slip the scrap of green velvet from my cloak hem and lay it on the desk. "The hem-end of what Corvin pocketed that night, my lord. I'd rather say the rest of it to you alone, since Tobin tells me this house has many ears." The scrap of velvet sits on the desk like a drop of old forest. Lord Edric stares at it. His hand rises, hovers, and finally touches it with one finger. His mouth works for a moment before any sound comes. "That... that is from the hall's own bolt. We never found the rest." His eyes lift, wet and bright. "You are the child."

Then you turn to the man in the corner, and your Insight check, a 21, tells you what the smile hides. It hasn't changed in all the time you've watched it. It's fixed, practised, and a little too exact. When the ribbon touched the desk his eyes went to the iron chest under the window, then to the door, then back, quick as a bird. He knew you were coming, and he knows who you are.

"Master Hale, steward and clerk of the household," the man says, rising with a small bow. His voice is soft and pleasant. "I keep my lord's accounts. And you, mistress, I gather, are the storyteller's apprentice. I must say my lord has been quite beside himself. Perhaps I should remain, to keep a record of whatever is agreed."

Lord Edric hesitates, glancing from you to his steward, and his hand closes over the ribbon. He's a man who has leaned on others for a long time. "Hale... leave us. A moment. I will call you."

"My lord," Hale says gently, "the matter of the assessor touches the whole house..."

"I said leave us."

Hale inclines his head. He goes slowly, and the door closes behind him with a soft, exact click. You hear his footsteps retreat along the corridor, but not quite all the way.

Tobin hovers by the hearth, miserable. Lord Edric looks at you with a lost, hopeful face. "Tell me, child. Is the charter lost? Can it be mended? What did Corvin do?"

You have a copy of the draft, the ledger in your psalter, and a tin of seal impressions. Hale may be listening at the door. What does Wren say or do?

I walk to the door and open it quickly, as if to check the corridor, and let Hale's listening ear be caught or at least startled. If he's there, I give him a sweet smile and say, "Master Hale, my lord asked for privacy, I'll fetch you myself." Then I shut it, and I tell Lord Edric in a low voice, "My lord, the charter's third descent is a forgery, and Corvin knows it will fail the assessor's inspection. I came to help you before it does, but first I need to know who else has seen the charter, and whether Hale has a copy."

You cross the room in three quick steps and swing the door wide. Master Hale is there, a pace from the frame with his head cocked, and for half a breath the smile is not on his face. Then it is, perfectly, as though it had never gone. "Master Hale," you say, sweet as honey, "my lord asked for privacy. I'll fetch you myself." He bows without a word, his eyes resting on yours a moment longer than they should. His footsteps go away down the corridor, and this time they keep going. You shut the door.

Lord Edric has sunk into his chair. When you tell him the third descent is a forgery, he doesn't protest. He just closes his eyes. "I thought it might be. I did not want to know." Then, in a low, hurried voice, he answers you.

Corvin sold him the charter as a restoration "from true records, long scattered." The whole line rests on the third descent, his grandsire's marriage into the old Aldermere house. Only four people have ever read the charter: himself, Corvin, old Brother Osric the chaplain, and Hale. Hale has the spare key, and Lord Edric admits, with a flush, that he once saw Hale's hand on the copy "for safekeeping." He thinks a scribe in Marrowford made a duplicate.

The assessor is Dame Ilsabet Crowe, who arrives at noon on the day after tomorrow. "She has broken two houses already," he says. "She says a forged line is a forged crown."

Tobin is staring at you from the hearth as though you might fix this by speaking. Lord Edric leans forward. "Can it be mended? I will pay whatever Corvin was owed, and more. I will not lose Thornhallow."

You have until noon on Day 4, a copy of Corvin's draft, a tin of seal impressions, and a ledger of his methods. Hale knows you're here. What does Wren say or do?

"It can be mended, my lord, but not by another forgery, not against someone like Dame Crowe. First, I need to see the charter itself and the old Aldermere marriage records, if your chaplain, Brother Osric, kept any, so I can build the repair on something true." I glance at Tobin. "And Tobin, keep watch on the corridor for me, quietly, and tell no one, Hale least of all, that I asked."

Tobin nods, slips out into the corridor, and pulls the door nearly closed behind him with a look of grim determination. Lord Edric fumbles a chain out from inside his collar and unlocks the iron chest under the window. The lid rises with a groan.

The charter is a long scroll of good vellum, heavy with ribbon-bound seals. You spread it on the desk and work through it by the window's light and a candle, tracing the descents one by one with a fingertip. Your Investigation check was a 9. The third descent is in a hand very close to the others, with the same iron-gall ink, aged with a tea-wash, and the vellum has been scraped and rewritten at the edges. You can tell it's wrong, but you can't tell *how* wrong. Was the marriage invented outright, or was it real and only its name or date altered? Without a true record to set beside it, you can't say.

Lord Edric watches you, hands knotted. "Brother Osric keeps the parish register in the chapel vestry, on the green," he says. "He's old and a little deaf, but he was here when my grandsire's marriage was supposedly made. If there's a true record anywhere, it's his."

Outside the window the sun is sliding west, and the village beyond the wall looks quiet. Tobin is in the corridor. Hale has gone somewhere. The assessor is a little over a day and a half away.

What does Wren do?

"Then I'll visit Brother Osric now, my lord, before Hale thinks to get there first." I copy the third descent's names and dates onto a fresh sheet, roll the charter back into its chest, and tell Lord Edric to lock it and keep the key on his neck. "Tobin, you're with me, and if anyone asks, I'm a pilgrim wanting to see the vestry and light a candle for the Lantern-Bearer."

You copy the third descent's names and dates onto a clean sheet, and Lord Edric rolls the charter back into the chest and locks it, the key going back inside his collar. Then you and Tobin slip out through the kitchen yard and across the green to the chapel.

It's a low stone building with a slate roof and a crooked bell-cote. In the porch burns a small brass wayside lamp, the sort travellers leave burning for the Lantern-Bearer, and your heart does an odd little turn at the sight of it. Inside it smells of beeswax and damp stone. Brother Osric is on his knees at a bench, a bent, white-haired man in a patched brown robe, polishing a pewter cup with great slowness.

You say your piece about the candle, the pilgrim, the vestry. Your Persuasion check was a 10, and it falls just short.

Osric's pale eyes lift. He cups one ear and makes you say it twice. Then he says, in a thin, careful voice, "Master Hale came by this morning. Said a clever young charlatan would come asking after my register. Said she'd talk sweetly." He doesn't say you're that charlatan. He doesn't say you aren't, either. He sets the cup down. "The register stays in the vestry, child. I don't open it to every pilgrim with a pretty tongue, however well she lights a candle."

He isn't hostile, only stubborn and afraid, and he's looking at the Lantern-Bearer's lamp in the porch as he says it. You carry a reliquary of that same god, and he hasn't seen it yet. Tobin shifts at your elbow, unsure whether to speak.

What does Wren do?

I drop the pilgrim act, kneel beside him, and take the brass lantern reliquary from my pack, setting it in his hands. "Hale's right that I'm a liar, Brother, and that's why I won't lie to you now: I stole this from a shrine wagon, and I've never known if the parchment inside is a true blessing or a forgery. You'd know a real one better than I would. Look at it, and then decide whether I get the register."

You kneel on the flagstones and set the little brass lantern in his knotted hands. You tell him what it is, where it came from, and that you've never known if what it holds is true. For a long moment Brother Osric says nothing. His thumb moves over the worn etching on the lid, a lamp with rays, and his lips shape a prayer you almost know.

He opens it with care and draws out the yellowed curl. The old man holds it close to the porch lamp's light and reads, slowly, tracing the lines with a fingertip. "That is a road-priest's hand," he says at last, very softly. "A real one. I trained beside a brother who wrote the same loops." He reads it aloud, and the words are plain: *"Let none who bear this lamp walk unlit. Let the false word fall from their tongue, and the true one light their road."* His eyes are wet. "Whoever wrote that meant it. It's a true blessing, child, and you carried it a long way without knowing."

You don't know what to do with your hands, so you hold still. Tobin looks away.

Osric returns the parchment to its case, folds your fingers around it, and gets to his feet with a groan. "Come."

In the vestry, from a chest under the altar stone, he lifts a thick register bound in cracked calfskin and a second, thinner copy written in his own cramped hand. He finds the page without searching, because he has read it many times. The entry is short. Aldous Verrel, grandsire of Lord Edric, married in this chapel by plain rite to Maud Fenn, miller's daughter of Thornhallow. There is no Aldermere in it, no great house, and no blood of the old line. Corvin changed the bride's name and her family.

"The manor was granted to the Verrels by plain deed," Osric says. "The descent was only ever for precedence and the tax-right. The land is theirs without it." He hesitates. "Master Hale asked to see this. I refused him."

It is five-twelve in the evening. You have the truth in hand, a day and a half before Dame Crowe arrives, and you can't be sure Hale hasn't another way into the chapel.

What does Wren do?

I copy the entry carefully onto a fresh sheet, and ask Brother Osric if he'd be willing to attest it in writing and in person before Dame Crowe. "DM: how many sheets of paper do I have left, and did I keep the dagger or just the rapier? I want to know what I can spare for a second copy."

You and Tobin step out onto the green with the light going amber. Your Perception check was a 12, and it catches what the dusk hides. By the village well stands a lean man in a plain brown tradesman's coat, doing nothing in particular, with an easy half-smile that doesn't reach his eyes. It's a smile you've seen before, or one very like it. As soon as you leave the chapel porch he turns away, unhurried, and heads for the manor gate, keeping to the shade of the wall.

Tobin has seen him too. His voice drops to a whisper. "That's... that's one of Hale's men. He came to the kitchens yesterday, asking for work." He swallows. "He's going to tell Hale where you've been."

The manor gate is a hundred paces off, and the man is already thirty ahead of you. Lord Edric is in his study with the chest and the key at his neck. Hale is in the house, and he knows you went to the chapel.

You carry the copy, Osric's promise, and Tobin's fear. What does Wren do?

"Tobin, run the back way through the kitchen yard to Lord Edric's study and tell him I'm coming and he's to lock the door and let no one in but me, not even Hale." I take the other path straight across the green at a brisk walk, cutting the brown-coated man off in the open before he reaches the gate, and call out warmly, "Friend! Forgive me, you look like a man who knows the way to the manor kitchens, I'm told there's supper there for pilgrims."
dice Wren's Deception check to delay the brown-coated man, DC 13: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [15] + 5 = 20

input.add_to_description: Gave his name as Garrow, a "hedge-carpenter looking for work", when Wren (Deception 20) walked him to the manor kitchens, delaying him ~15 minutes. Let slip that he came upriver from Marrowford the same day as Wren and "keeps an eye on the road for the steward."

transcript.result: added to Smiling Follower's description; Smiling Follower is also called Garrow

transcript.text: notebook: updated Smiling Follower
time: 15 minutes later: Day 2, 6:07 PM

Tobin goes off like a startled hare, pelting for the kitchen yard, and you take the long way across the open green at an easy, unhurried pace, cutting the angle neatly. Your Deception check was a 20.

"Friend!" you call, warm as a hearth. "Forgive me, you look like a man who knows the way to the kitchens. I'm told there's supper for pilgrims."

The brown-coated man stops. His smile doesn't waver, but you see him weigh the thing, an honest pilgrim and a dozen eyes on the green. He lets the moment go. "Garrow, mistress. Hedge-carpenter, looking for work." He glances toward the gate, then back at you. "The kitchens are this way, aye. Round by the dovecote."

You walk him there, chatting the whole way about the Marrow's ferries, the price of bread, a pilgrim's blisters, and the smile slowly becomes a puzzled, polite thing. He lets slip that he came upriver from Marrowford the same day you did, and that he "keeps an eye on the road for the steward," then catches himself and laughs it off. By the time you reach the kitchen door, a quarter of an hour has gone, and Tobin has had all the time he needed.

The kitchen is warm, loud with pans and a spit turning over a fire. As you step in, a figure rises from a bench by the wall, neat and soft-voiced and smiling: Master Hale. He's holding a cup of cider as though he'd been there all evening.

"Mistress Ashgrove," he says pleasantly. "My lord is indisposed. He's asked not to be disturbed. Perhaps you'd care to sit and take supper with me, and we might talk like sensible people."

Behind him, through the passage, you can hear a door slam and a bolt shoot. That's Lord Edric's study, and Tobin got there first.

What does Wren do?

I give Hale my brightest grin and sit right down across from him, helping myself to a heel of bread. "Sensible people, Master Hale, my favourite kind. Let's talk, then: you tell me what you think I came here for, and I'll tell you whether you're warm or cold."

While he answers, I'll keep my hands in plain sight on the table and watch his eyes for what he reaches for first, the chest, the door, or his purse.
dice Wren's Insight check watching Hale's tells as he talks, DC 14: 1d20+3 = 1d20 [1] + 3 = 4 (natural 1)

input.add_to_description: Day 2 evening in the Thornhallow kitchen: Hale offers Wren a "sensible" bargain: hand over Corvin's ledger from her road-psalter and he will see Lord Edric's charter "quietly made right" and pay her well. Reality: Hale has been Corvin's inside man in House Verrel for years, selling Corvin word of what clients can pay; he wants the ledger so no one can trace the forgeries or his share. Wren's natural-1 Insight misread him as bluffing and unsure what she carries; in fact Hale knows exactly that the ledger is hidden in the psalter's binding (Garrow saw it in Marrowford inn).

transcript.result: added to Master Hale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Master Hale
time: 10 minutes later: Day 2, 6:17 PM

You sit and take the bread, and Hale folds his hands on the table with a look of mild, pleased attention. The cook clatters pans at the far end of the kitchen, out of hearing. Your Insight check was a natural 1, so what you read in him may well be wrong.

You think you see his eyes drift to the door and linger there, and his fingers twitch against his cup. To you he looks uncertain, like a man bluffing who isn't sure what you carry or what you know.

"Mistress Ashgrove," he says, gently. "I think you came to Thornhallow for the same reason as I did, to take care of my lord. I don't intend any harm to him or to you. Corvin Tallowmere's work has made a great many people comfortable. It would be a shame if it were... *disturbed*." He lets that sit. "I understand you carry something of his in your road-psalter. A book. If you let me look at it, I'll see that the charter is made right, quietly and kindly, without any assessor's help. And you would be well paid."

His smile never changes. He doesn't ask whether you have it. He just says where it is.

The smell of bread and onions fills the room, and the spit turns. Through the passage you hear nothing from Lord Edric's study. Tobin is behind that bolted door, and Garrow has slipped in by the dovecote entrance to stand near the pantry, not quite watching you.

What does Wren say or do?

I laugh softly and tear off a piece of bread. "Master Hale, you flatter me. The psalter's not on me, it's with a friend in Marrowford who has instructions to carry it straight to Dame Crowe if I'm not back to fetch it by noon on the day after tomorrow, so I'd think carefully about anything unkind happening to me or my lord's household." I smile sweetly. "Now, since we're being sensible, who exactly pays me well, you or whoever is paying you?"
dice Wren's Deception check bluffing Hale about the psalter and a friend in Marrowford, DC 15 (Hale is sharp and suspects it's on her): 1d20+5 = 1d20 [3] + 5 = 8

input.add_to_description: Wren's Deception (8) failed to convince him her ledger is elsewhere. He pointed out that Garrow saw her put the psalter back in her pack at the Drowned Candle. He nodded to Garrow, who now stands at the kitchen's back door. Hale did not draw a weapon; he wants the book without scandal.

transcript.result: added to Master Hale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Master Hale
time: 2 minutes later: Day 2, 6:19 PM

You laugh, you spin it, and you ask your clever closing question. Your Deception check was an 8 against his sharpness, and it doesn't land.

Hale's smile doesn't change, but his eyes warm very slightly, the way a cat's might. "That's a lovely story, mistress. A friend in Marrowford." He takes a sip of cider. "I'd wager you've no friend in Marrowford at all. Garrow here saw you stow that psalter back in your pack at the Drowned Candle, and I rather think it hasn't left your side since." He doesn't look at Garrow, but he nods very slightly. By the back door, the carpenter shifts a pace to stand across the exit, hands loose, still wearing his easy smile.

"I don't want to hurt anyone," Hale says. "Truly. A book, a quiet word, and your road in the morning. My lord keeps his manor, you keep your head and a pouch of silver. The alternative is that the assessor arrives to find a girl who stole a ledger from a respected storyteller and bribed a country chaplain to counterfeit a register." He spreads his hands. "Which of us do you think she'd believe?"

The kitchen is warm, loud, ordinary, a cook with her back turned and a boy scraping pots. Nobody has drawn a weapon. The study's bolted door is thirty paces down the passage. Garrow is at the back door and Hale is across the table, calm, hands visible.

What does Wren do?

I stand up, push the stool back loudly, and pitch my voice to carry across the whole kitchen. "Master Hale, did I hear that right? You'll pay me a pouch of silver to hand over my lord's papers and be gone before the assessor comes?" I turn to the cook and the pot-boy with a bright, scandalized look. "Good people, you're all witnesses to the steward of Thornhallow offering a bribe to a pilgrim!"

Then I keep my hand off my rapier and walk steadily down the passage toward Lord Edric's study, calling, "My lord, it's Wren, open the door, the whole kitchen's heard your steward!"
dice Wren's Performance check playing the kitchen and the room, DC 12: 1d20+5 = 1d20 [7] + 5 = 12

input.add_to_description: Publicly exposed in the kitchen at Thornhallow (Day 2, ~6:25 PM) by Wren's Performance (12): the cook, a pot-boy and a kitchen-maid heard him offer a pouch of silver to Wren to hand over "my lord's papers" and leave before the assessor came. Hale denied it with perfect calm ("a misunderstanding"), but he cannot now act openly in front of the household.

transcript.result: added to Master Hale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Master Hale
time: 5 minutes later: Day 2, 6:24 PM

The stool scrapes loudly and your voice rings across the kitchen like a bell. Your Performance check was a 12, just enough. The cook's ladle stops. The pot-boy's scraping stops. A kitchen-maid by the window turns with wide eyes, and every face in the room swings to Master Hale.

For the first time since you met him, the smile slips, only for a moment, a flicker of stone under the water. "A misunderstanding," Hale says evenly. "The pilgrim's overtired. I was merely..."

But the room has already decided. The cook folds her arms. The pot-boy mutters, "I heard 'silver,'" and nobody tells him to hush. Garrow, by the back door, shifts uneasily and glances at his master, and he doesn't step to block you. He can't do it in front of twelve pairs of eyes.

You walk down the passage steadily, hand well clear of the rapier, calling Lord Edric's name. Behind you Hale's chair scrapes and his soft, even footsteps follow at a polite distance. You reach the study door and hear the bolt rasp. It swings open an inch, then wide, and Tobin's pale face appears, and behind him Lord Edric stands with the key chain clutched at his neck.

"Child?" he says. "What is it? What did they hear?"

Hale arrives at your shoulder, composed again, hands folded. "My lord," he says quietly, "the girl has been telling tales in the kitchens. I thought it best to attend you."

The room is quiet. You hold the copy of the register entry and Osric's promise, and Lord Edric is looking from one of you to the other. What does Wren say or do?

I step inside and put the register copy straight into Lord Edric's hands, then stay between him and Hale. "My lord, read this first. Your grandsire Aldous married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter, in your own chapel, and Brother Osric will swear to it before Dame Crowe. The land is yours by plain deed, and the Aldermere line was Corvin's invention."

I turn to Hale with a bright smile. "And while you read, my lord, ask your steward why he wanted the book in my psalter, and why a man who 'merely attends' brought a hedge-carpenter named Garrow from Marrowford."

input.add_to_description: Day 2 evening: read the register copy, accepted that the land is his by plain deed and the Aldermere line was invented. Ordered Hale to stay in the study while Edric questions him. Hale, cornered, said Wren stole Corvin's ledger and that he's been "protecting" the house from her. Edric now looks to Wren to explain the ledger.

transcript.result: added to Lord Edric Verrel's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Lord Edric Verrel
time: 10 minutes later: Day 2, 6:34 PM

Lord Edric takes the sheet with both hands and reads it standing by the window, lips moving. Twice he stops, then goes back to the top. When he looks up his face has changed. It isn't the grey, hunted look any more, but something older and quieter.

"Aldous married Maud Fenn," he says. "My grandmother. I remember her hands. She smelled of flour." He laughs, a short, wet, startled sound. "I was ashamed of nothing. And Corvin sold me a shame to carry." He lowers the paper. "The land is mine by plain deed?"

"By a deed older than the charter, my lord. Osric will swear to it."

Then Lord Edric turns to Hale, who hasn't moved from your shoulder, and for the first time the steward's smile has gone entirely. In its place is an expression you can't read, a flat, thoughtful look.

"Hale. The book in her psalter. The man Garrow."

Hale lets out a slow breath. "My lord," he says quietly, "I'll be plain, since the girl has made plainness fashionable. Corvin Tallowmere's ledger is a record of the forgeries he sold to three houses. It would ruin Verrel in the right hands, and Dame Crowe's would be the right hands. This girl stole it from her master and has carried it here. I have been trying, for your sake, to take it from a thief and burn it before it harmed you." His eyes slide to you. "Ask her if it's true that she took it. Ask her what she means to do with it."

Tobin makes a small, frightened sound by the hearth. The kitchen has gathered quietly in the passage, listening. Lord Edric looks at you, and his voice is gentle, almost afraid. "Child. Is it so? Do you have Corvin's ledger?"

The lie that would be easiest isn't what any of them are waiting for. What does Wren say or do?

"Yes, my lord, I have it, and I'll not lie to you about that." I take the psalter from my pack, work the binding open, and slide out only the Verrel pages. "I took the ledger because I couldn't stomach what Corvin had done, and I came to find the people he'd cheated. This is your house's page. Burn it in the hearth, my lord, in front of everyone, because it's yours to burn, not Hale's."

I close the psalter again and look at Hale. "The other pages belong to two other houses, and I'll decide what's right for them myself, not by a steward's say-so. But I notice he wanted it burned *before* you saw it, and you're the one it concerns."
sheet: XP +100: 100

input.add_to_description: Day 2 ~7 PM: Verrel ledger page bore Hale's marginal initials and sums, his cut as Corvin's informant inside the house. Lord Edric burned the page himself in the study hearth, then had Hale locked in the cellar store under guard of the old gate-guard until the assessor comes. Garrow slipped over the wall in the confusion and fled upriver toward Marrowford, presumably to warn Corvin.

transcript.result: added to Master Hale's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Master Hale

input.add_to_description: Day 2 ~7 PM: Lord Edric burned the Verrel ledger page. Hale confined; Garrow fled toward Marrowford to warn Corvin. Remaining: Dame Crowe arrives noon Day 4 (Lord Edric to confess the plain truth with Osric's attestation); Corvin will return; two other houses in the ledger (names not yet read) are still owed truth or restitution.

transcript.result: added to The Sealed Letter's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Sealed Letter
time: 40 minutes later: Day 2, 7:14 PM

You don't flinch. You take out the psalter, work the stitched binding open with a thumbnail, and slide free a single folded leaf, then close the book again in plain view of the whole passage. The room stays utterly still.

"This is your house's page, my lord. It's yours to burn, not Hale's."

Lord Edric unfolds it. Corvin's neat hand lists dates, the sum paid and the descent altered. In the margin, in a smaller and different ink, run neat little initials and tallies: *H. — 2s. in the pound.* He reads them through, and you watch his shoulders go slowly straight.

"Two shillings in the pound," he says. "Out of my own purse."

He crosses to the hearth and drops the page onto the coals. It curls, browns, blooms briefly orange, and is gone. No one speaks. Then he turns to the doorway. "Master Hale will wait in the cellar store with the gate-guard at the door until the assessor comes. Nobody will lay a hand on him. Nobody will leave him without bread and water." His voice cracks only a little. "Take him."

Hale goes without a word, the smile folded away like a handkerchief. In the confusion Garrow is gone, over the dovecote wall into the dusk. Tobin thinks he went toward the Marrowford road, probably to carry word upriver to Corvin.

Lord Edric sits down heavily. He looks at you for a long time. "I'll tell Dame Crowe the plain truth," he says, "with Osric's name beside mine. If I lose the precedence, I lose it. A miller's granddaughter's bread was never a shameful thing." Then, softly: "What do I owe you, child?"

You have gained 100 XP, bringing you to 100 of 300. It's a quarter past seven on Day 2. Corvin is somewhere upriver and may learn that his forgery has failed, and two other houses in your psalter are still owed the truth.

What does Wren do?

I shake my head with a crooked smile. "Nothing, my lord, but a bed for the night, a hot supper, and two promises: that you'll keep Osric safe until the assessor comes, and that if a storyteller named Corvin shows up here, you'll send word to me before you open the door." I glance at the psalter in my hands. "The other two houses in this book are next, and I'd like to know their names and where they hold, so I'll sleep, then start on them at first light."

input.description: Minor house of Lady Maren Thistlewood at Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford. Corvin forged her a tale of a heroic ancestor holding a river ford, to claim ferry-toll rights. Already paid; page struck through in Corvin's draft. Toll rights are being contested by neighbouring village.

input.add_to_description: Day 2 night: Wren read the two other pages. House Thistlewood (Lady Maren, Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford; forged ford/toll tale) and House Dray (Sir Corwen, Saltmarsh Keep, estuary three days downriver; forged betrothal contract). Both paid and "struck through" in Corvin's draft; Corvin planned to mend only Verrel.

transcript.result: added to The Sealed Letter's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Sealed Letter
time: 11 hours 45 minutes later: Day 3, 6:59 AM

Lord Edric stares, then laughs shakily. "A bed, a supper, and two promises. Child, I'd have given you the south field." But he gives his word on both, hand on the table. Osric will be fetched to the manor under guard that very night, and if a storyteller named Corvin comes to the gate, a rider will find you before the door opens.

Supper is mutton and barley bread and a cup of cider, eaten at the kitchen table among cooks who now treat you like a visiting saint, or perhaps like a small, dangerous animal. Tobin sits at your elbow and doesn't say much, but he keeps pushing the best bits of the mutton toward you. He's asleep on a bench before the cider is gone. You're given a clean bed in a small room under the eaves.

Before sleeping you spread the two remaining leaves under a candle. The names are there in Corvin's neat hand. Lady Maren Thistlewood of Ashby Weir, two days upriver of Marrowford, was sold a hero's tale of an ancestor who held the ford, to claim ferry-toll rights. Sir Corwen Dray of Saltmarsh Keep, out on the estuary some three days downriver of here, bought a betrothal contract and a vow-tale tying his heir to a wealthy merchant family, and those merchants have begun to doubt. Both pages are struck through as paid. Corvin meant to mend only Verrel.

You sleep, and the night is quiet. It's just before seven now on Day 3, with the sun rising over a clean, cold morning. The assessor arrives tomorrow at noon. Corvin is somewhere upriver, and Garrow has had most of a night's start toward him.

What does Wren do?

I pack my psalter, thank the kitchen for the mutton, and find Lord Edric before breakfast. "My lord, lend me a mule and a short letter in your hand saying I act with your blessing. I'm going upriver through Marrowford to Lady Thistlewood at Ashby Weir, because that's where Corvin will be heading once Garrow finds him, and I'd rather meet him on my road than on his." On my way out I give Tobin a wink and slip him the last of my bread. "Keep your head down, Tobin, and if Osric needs anything, you're his legs."
sheet: lost 1 × Bread loaf; gained 1 × Letter under Lord Edric Verrel's seal, vouching for Wren; gained 1 × Mule (lent by Lord Edric Verrel)

input.add_to_description: Day 3 ~1:30 PM: gone from Marrowford's square. A fishwife reports Garrow (brown coat) arrived at dawn on a lathered horse, spoke to the driver, and the wagon left at once north-upriver on the Ashby road with the driver whipping the team. Strongbox and everything went with it.

transcript.result: added to Corvin's Wagon's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin's Wagon
time: 6 hours 30 minutes later: Day 3, 1:29 PM

Lord Edric is at the kitchen table in his shirt-sleeves with a bowl of porridge, looking ten years younger. He hears you through, nods, and writes the letter himself with an ink-stained thumb and a flourish, sealing it with his signet in green wax. "To all whom it concerns: the bearer, Wren Ashgrove, acts with my full blessing and my gratitude." He also has the stable-boy saddle a placid grey mule called Biscuit.

Tobin takes the last of your bread with both hands, as if it were a medal, and nods fiercely. "I'll be Brother Osric's legs. I promise." Then, lower: "Thank you. For not being smiling."

You ride out of the gate into the cold bright morning with the Marrow glinting at your left hand. The road upriver is the same one you walked down, but it looks different under a mule's nodding head, wide and ordinary and slow. By half past one you're clattering over the stone bridge into Marrowford.

The square is busy with market-day trade, but your eye goes at once to the far corner. The place where Corvin's painted wagon stood is empty, with only a scatter of straw and a dark patch of oil on the cobbles. A fishwife by the tailor's stall sees you looking and wipes her hands. "Looking for the shrine-wagon, love? Gone at dawn. A man in a brown coat came in on a lathered horse, shouted at the driver, and off they went up the Ashby road like the river was on fire." She sniffs. "Strongbox and all."

So Garrow got word and the wagon moved, and the wagon is now on the road to Ashby Weir, the same road you meant to take, an hour or two of start ahead of you and a team of horses to your mule. It's half past one on Day 3.

What does Wren do?

I toss the fishwife a copper and lean down from Biscuit's back. "Thank you, love. Was Corvin himself aboard, or only the driver and the man in the brown coat, and did either of them ask after a young woman with a lute?" Then I turn the mule toward the Ashby road, keeping to a steady walk so I don't spend him, and think it over as I go: the wagon is hours ahead, so I'd rather arrive after them and watch Lady Thistlewood's gate than ride in on their heels.

DM: how much coin do I have now, and is the tinker's set of thieves' tools still 25 gp if I pass back through here?
sheet: money -1 cp: now 14 gp 6 sp 1 cp

input.description: Small wayside shrine-house of the Lantern-Bearer on the Ashby road, half a day's ride north of Marrowford. A stone hut with a bunkroom, a hearth, and a brass lamp kept lit. Run by a lay-keeper named Marta Pell, a cheerful widow. Offers free bed and bread to Lantern-Bearer faithful (Wren's Shelter of the Faithful).
relationships: on the road between [[Marrowford]] and Ashby Weir

transcript.result: entry Lantern's Rest (place) created; relationship [22] added to Lantern's Rest

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Lantern's Rest; added 1 relationship to Lantern's Rest
time: 5 hours 10 minutes later: Day 3, 6:39 PM

You flip her a copper and she snatches it neatly out of the air. "Only the driver and the brown-coated one," she says. "Not the master, not that I saw. The brown coat asked the stall-folk whether a young half-elf with a lute had come through, and he wasn't sweet about it. Sharp-faced fellow. Take care, love."

You have 14 gp 6 sp 1 cp now, down a copper. And the tinker, if you ask, still wants his 25 gp for the thieves' tools. He hasn't moved his tray, and it's the same price, so it's out of reach for now.

You turn Biscuit up the Ashby road at an easy walk and let the afternoon pass. The road climbs away from the river, runs through hop fields, then oak woods, then open heath. You keep the pace steady and the mule unhurried, watching for dust or wheel-ruts. About half past six, with the sky going the colour of a bruise, a thin thread of smoke and a small glowing lamp appear ahead where the road forks.

It's a squat stone shrine-house with a tiled roof and a lantern hung on a pole by its door, a brass lamp with rays carved into the shutters, the Lantern-Bearer's sign. A hand-painted board by the gate says **LANTERN'S REST: BED, BREAD, AND A LIGHT FOR ANY WHO WALK.** A plump, grey-haired woman in a green apron is raking the yard and looks up as you approach.

There are fresh wheel-ruts in the soft ground by the gate, two wheels, heavy, turned in and out. Wagon ruts, and recent.

What does Wren do?

I dismount, pat Biscuit's neck, and walk up with the reliquary held openly in my palm so the lamp catches its brass. "Evening, Mother. A traveler of the Lantern-Bearer asks shelter for herself and a mule, and if you've bread to spare, I'd be glad of it." Then, glancing at the ruts, lightly: "Looks like a wagon came through ahead of me. Did a shrine-wagon stop here, and did its driver say where they'd sleep?"

input.add_to_description: Day 3: Corvin lodged at Lantern's Rest the night before and joined his wagon there at noon, charming the keeper Marta Pell. He left a sealed note for "a young woman with a lute" (Wren) in Marta's keeping, then took the wagon toward Ashby Weir with Garrow and the driver. He seems to have expected her.

transcript.result: added to Corvin Tallowmere's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

input.add_to_description: Keeper Marta Pell, grey-haired, plump, green apron, warm and talkative. Corvin is a regular guest and has charmed her; she holds his sealed note for Wren. She gives Wren free bed and bread as a follower of the Lantern-Bearer.

transcript.result: added to Lantern's Rest's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Lantern's Rest
sheet: gained 1 × Sealed note from Corvin Tallowmere (unopened)
time: 15 minutes later: Day 3, 6:54 PM

The woman's face crinkles into a smile at the sight of the little brass lantern. "Bless me, a real one! Marta Pell, keeper here these fourteen years. Come in, love, come in. There's a bunk and a bowl of barley broth and your mule can have the lean-to." She takes Biscuit's rein herself and clucks at him like an old friend. The bed and the bread are free, as the shrine's custom is for any of the faithful.

As she leads the mule round the side, she answers you without needing to be asked twice. The wagon came through at noon, painted lantern and all, with a brown-coated man shouting at the driver. "But Master Tallowmere was already here. He's lodged with me the night before, the dear man, and he's been coming through these seven years. He gave that lamp over the door." She nods to the brass lantern. "He said he'd a lady to see about a ford, up at Ashby Weir, and took the wagon straight on. Left in a great hurry, the brown one in a terrible taking."

She stops, wipes her hands on her apron, and fishes in a pocket. "And he left this for a young woman with a lute, if she should come by. 'Tall, half-elf, quick with a smile,' he said. I thought you'd be her the moment you rode up." She pushes a small, folded square of vellum into your hand, sealed with a blob of blue wax and the shrine-lantern stamped on it.

Inside, a fire crackles in the hearth, and the smell of barley broth drifts out. Corvin knew you were coming, or guessed. He stayed one step ahead of you here.

You can open the note now, take a moment with Marta first, or sleep on it. What does Wren do?

I check the seal carefully under the lamp for signs of tampering or anything odd, like a pin-prick, powder or a trap, then break the wax and read it by the lantern's light. Whatever it says, I'll keep my face still, because Marta's watching and I'd like to hear it from my own head first.
dice Wren's Investigation check examining the seal and vellum for tampering or a trap, DC 12: 1d20+2 = 1d20 [3] + 2 = 5

time: 10 minutes later: Day 3, 7:04 PM

You turn the little square of vellum under the lamp, searching for a pin-prick, a dusting of powder, a thread of poison. Your Investigation check was a 5, and you can't tell either way. The wax looks ordinary, the vellum smells faintly of his clove-and-ink, and you can't be sure of anything.

You break it with your thumbnail anyway, keep your face still, and read in the lantern's light. Marta is polishing a cup and pretending not to watch.

*Wren, my girl.*

*You took the wrong book. I'm not angry. A father isn't angry when a clever child proves she's clever. Come to the ford at Ashby Weir at dusk on the fifth day, alone, and bring it. We'll talk like family and see what can be mended, you and I, before someone less gentle than I am gets the idea of reading it for themselves.*

*One thing more, for the road. That curl of parchment in your little brass lantern is not my work. I never wrote it. Ask yourself who did, and why I let you carry it all this way.*

*C.* There's a tiny drawn lantern beneath the initial.

The room feels quiet in a strange way. He knew about the reliquary, and about the parchment. He's telling you it's real, and that he let you keep it, and nothing about that note is the voice of a man who thinks he has lost.

The fifth day is two days away. The wagon is somewhere on the Ashby road, and Lady Thistlewood's gate is a day's ride past this fork. Marta has set a bowl of barley broth by the hearth for you.

What does Wren do?

I fold the note, tuck it into the psalter next to the ledger pages, and sit down to the broth with a calm face. "Mother Pell, you've known Corvin seven years. Did he ever mention who gave him the brass lantern-case, or a road-priest who wrote blessings in a looped hand? I'd also like a look at the lamp he gave you, if you'll let me, and I'll tell you a good story for it after supper."

You fold the note into the psalter beside the ledger pages and sit to the broth like a girl with nothing on her mind. Marta settles across from you with her mending.

She thinks a moment. "Who gave him the lantern-case? He never said, love. But I'll tell you something. The first year he stopped here, he sat up all night over that brass lamp over my door, turning it in his hands and saying, 'The same hand, Marta. The same hand.' I took it for a figure of speech." She nods at the lamp. "Take it down, if you like. It's no use hanging up there to be admired."

The lamp comes down on a stool, and you turn it in the firelight. Your Religion check was a 14. The brass is old and soft with age, with cast rays on the shutters like the ones on your own reliquary, and on the base, so tiny you almost miss it, a scratched mark. It's a lantern with a crooked flame and two letters, *E.A.*, in the same looped hand as the blessing in your reliquary. Whoever made one made the other, and Corvin got both.

You tell Marta a story for the lamp, one about a tinker's daughter and a lantern that wouldn't go out, and she laughs and wipes her eyes at the end. The fire burns down. She puts you in the bunkroom, alone, and the shutters are barred. Biscuit snuffles in the lean-to.

It's near eight now on Day 3. The assessor reaches Thornhallow tomorrow at noon. Corvin's rendezvous is dusk on Day 5. The wagon is a few hours ahead on the road. You haven't decided yet whether to rest here or ride on.

What does Wren do?

I decide to sleep here, since I'll be no use to anyone half-dead on a mule, but first I copy the "E.A." mark and the crooked-flame lantern onto a scrap of paper to keep in the psalter. Then I ask Marta whether any road-priest named E.A. ever passed through, or whether there's an old shrine register or a travelers' book here I could skim in the morning.

You copy the lantern-with-the-crooked-flame and the two looped letters onto a scrap and tuck it into the psalter. Marta frowns, then shakes her head. No road-priest named E.A. that she knows, but there is the shrine's travellers' book on the shelf above the hearth, kept since before her time, and you're welcome to it in the morning.

You sleep. The bunk is narrow and the blankets smell of lavender and woodsmoke, and no dreams trouble you. At dawn Marta brings hot porridge and a heel of cheese, and the book, a fat, battered volume with a cracked leather spine. You're rested, your spells and Bardic Inspiration are restored, and the clock reads half past six.

You turn the pages carefully. Your Investigation check was an 11, but it's enough to find what's wrong: the leaves for the season about twenty years back have been cut out with a blade. The cuts are clean, close to the stitching, and the stitching has gone dark with age. Marta never noticed. She took over the shrine fourteen years ago. "Old Hob Crannock kept it before me," she says, frowning at the gap. "Retired to a cottage by the ford at Ashby Weir. He'd remember. Though his wits go in and out like the tide."

The ford at Ashby Weir is where Corvin wants to meet you on the fifth day. The assessor, if Lord Edric has told the truth, arrives at Thornhallow at noon today. Biscuit is fed and saddled in the yard, and the Ashby road runs north under a white morning mist.

What does Wren do?

I thank Marta, leave a silver piece in the shrine's offering box despite the free bed, and ride out on Biscuit toward Ashby Weir. I'll look for old Hob Crannock's cottage by the ford first, before Corvin's wagon or Lady Thistlewood, and keep an eye out for Garrow's brown coat on the road.

input.description: Small river village on the upper Marrow where the old stone weir and ford cross; seat of House Thistlewood (Lady Maren). Ferry-toll bridge disputed. Old Hob Crannock's cottage lies by the ford. A reed-thatched inn, the Heron and Net.

time: 10 hours 30 minutes later: Day 4, 5:00 PM

You drop a silver piece in the shrine's offering box despite the free bed, and Marta presses a warm bun into your hand with a look that says she'll pray for you whether you ask or not. Then Biscuit plods out onto the Ashby road under the white morning mist.

The road climbs through heath, dips into oak woods, and follows a stream. You keep your eyes open for a brown coat or a flash of the wagon's painted lantern, but your Perception check was a 3, and the road gives you nothing. Biscuit eats the miles patiently. You rest him at noon by a trough, and the afternoon lengthens. If someone is watching from the copses, you wouldn't know it.

By five in the evening the road tops a low rise and the land opens. Below lies Ashby Weir. A long, low stone weir holds back a pale gleam of river, and downstream of it the ford spreads wide and shallow, studded with stepping stones. A cluster of thatched cottages leans along the bank, with smoke rising from them and a larger inn, the Heron and Net, at the centre. Upstream, a grey manor house stands on a spur among willows, the Thistlewood seat. Nearer, at the water's edge by the ford, a small crooked cottage with a green door sits beside a heap of lobster pots and a drying rack of nets.

There's no wagon in sight. There's no sign of Corvin. The ford is two days of walking from Marrowford, and you've made it with a day to spare. Dusk is two hours away.

What does Wren do?

I leave Biscuit tied at the lobster pots, knock on the green door, and call out in a friendly, unhurried voice, "Master Crannock? A traveler of the Lantern-Bearer, sent by Mother Pell at Lantern's Rest, who says you keep the best memory on the river." If he opens, I'll hold up the reliquary and the sketch of the crooked-flame E.A. lantern, and ask him about the pages cut from the shrine book twenty years back.

time: 40 minutes later: Day 4, 5:40 PM

You tie Biscuit among the lobster pots and knock on the green door. Nothing, then a shuffle, then the bolt. The door opens a hand's width on a face like a dried apple, with white whiskers and bright, watery eyes. "Who's that? Is it the tax-man?"

"A traveler of the Lantern-Bearer, sent by Mother Pell, who says you keep the best memory on the river." You hold up the reliquary so the dying sun catches its rays, and then the sketch. Your Persuasion check was a 13, and the eyes sharpen.

"The crooked flame," he whispers. The door opens, and he draws you into a smoky room that smells of tar and pipe-weed. He sits you by the hearth and takes the sketch in a shaking hand, and for a moment you think his wits have drifted off. Then they come back like a boat on a tide.

"Elowen," he says. "Elowen Ashgrove. A road-priest of the Lantern, proper, with a lamp-staff and a looped hand. She came through the shrine twenty years back with a babe wrapped in a green blanket, hungry and cold, and she asked me to cut the book's pages for that season. I said it was a sin, and she said it was a mercy. So I did, with her own knife." He wipes his eye. "She left the lamp over the door, and a curl of blessing in a little brass case, and said she was going upriver to Ashby Weir, to a house she trusted. And that was the last of her. I never saw her again."

His gaze settles on your face for a long moment. "A storyteller came asking after her the next spring. Silver-tongued. Too many questions. I told him nothing, and he went off sulking. That would have been your Master Tallowmere, would it?"

He says her surname the same way the world has said yours since you were small. *Ashgrove.* You have no memory of a name before it, and the old man is watching your face for what you'll do with it.

Dusk is over an hour away. You could ask him what house she trusted, what became of the baby, or who else knew. What does Wren do?

My voice comes out smaller than I mean it to, and I hold the reliquary a little tighter. "Master Crannock, which house did she trust? Was it the Thistlewoods up on the spur, and the babe in the green blanket... was there a ribbon with it, green velvet?" I take the scrap from my cloak hem and lay it on his knee. "Please, take your time. I'd rather have it slow and true than quick."

He believes Elowen left the child in Lady Agnes's keeping; some months later a storyteller (Corvin) turned up on the Marrowford road with a girl-child of about that age, claiming he found her at a roadside shrine. Hob never saw Elowen again and does not know what became of her. Hob also says Lady Maren is not a bad woman, but afraid of the village over the toll.

time: 30 minutes later: Day 4, 6:10 PM

You lay the scrap of green velvet on his knee and tell him to take his time. The old man doesn't touch it at first. He looks at it for a long while with his mouth working, and the fire pops, and a gull cries on the weir. You wait.

"Green velvet," he says at last, very softly. "Aye. The blanket was edged in it, deep as moss, a good bolt, a noble's cloth. It was too fine for a priest's baby. I remember thinking that." He lifts the scrap with one thumb and forefinger as if it might bruise. "She said she was going to the lady on the spur. Old Lady Agnes Thistlewood, the grandmother of the house, may she rest. She was kind. Good to the road. Elowen said, 'Agnes will keep her safe till I can come back.'" His voice thins. "But she never came back, as far as I ever heard, and I don't know what Lady Agnes did with the child. Only..."

He frowns, hunting for the thread. "Some months after, a storyteller came down the Marrowford road with a little girl of about that age on his cart. Said he found her at a roadside shrine, wrapped in a blanket. Pretty talker. I thought nothing of it then." He looks up at you and doesn't say the rest, because he doesn't need to.

"Lady Maren rules the spur now, her daughter," he adds. "A fair woman, but afraid of the village over the ferry-toll, and not much liked. She was only a girl herself then. She might remember, or she might not."

The fire burns low. Outside, the light has turned gold and slanting over the ford. It's ten past six, and dusk is an hour away. Corvin's meeting is tomorrow at dusk, and the Thistlewood house is on the spur above the village.

What does Wren do?

I thank Hob warmly, tuck the scrap of velvet back into my hem, and ask him one more thing: whether he'd be willing to speak for Elowen's mark if a lady asked him. Then I ride Biscuit up the spur to the Thistlewood gate, with Lord Edric's sealed letter in hand and the psalter pages for Lady Maren's house at the ready, and ask to see her tonight on a matter of her family's honor and her mother's kindness to a road-priest.

input.description: Mistress of the Thistlewood manor at Ashby Weir, a tired, straight-backed woman in her forties, daughter of old Lady Agnes. Afraid of her village over the ferry-toll, which rests on Corvin's forged ford tale. Received Wren at dusk on Day 4 after reading Lord Edric's letter.

time: 50 minutes later: Day 4, 7:00 PM

Hob nods, slow and certain. "If a lady asks me, I'll say what I saw, and swear it on Elowen's lamp. I owe her that." He walks you to the green door and watches you go.

The spur path winds up through willows, and Biscuit takes it without complaint. The gatehouse of the Thistlewood manor is shut for the evening. A pair of tired-looking men-at-arms in faded blue peer down at you, and your Persuasion check was a 13. Lord Edric's green-waxed letter does most of the work, passed up on the point of a halberd and carried inside. You wait with the mule among the cooling stones while the dusk gathers, and a bat flits over the wall. Then the wicket opens.

You're led across a small, worn courtyard into a long, panelled hall, hung with faded banners and a single great painting of a stern man at a ford, with the river gleaming behind him, the hero of Corvin's tale, you realise. At the far end, by a fire too large for the room's warmth, sits a straight-backed woman in her forties in a grey gown, with ink-stained fingers and a worn expression of guarded politeness. This is Lady Maren Thistlewood.

She has your letter open on her knee. "Lord Edric Verrel writes that the bearer acts with his blessing," she says. "He doesn't say why. I'm told you spoke of my mother's kindness to a road-priest." Her gaze is steady, a little tired. "I'm not often visited by anyone at this hour who isn't asking for the toll. Sit, Mistress Ashgrove. I'd like to hear what you have to say."

You have the ledger pages in your psalter, Hob's story, and Corvin's note. Corvin himself meets you tomorrow at dusk. Somewhere out in the dark Garrow's eyes may be on you.

What does Wren say?

I sit, keep my hands visible, and tell her plainly. "My lady, I'm a storyteller's apprentice, and I've come to give you the truth about the hero at the ford in that painting: Corvin Tallowmere sold your family a tale, and I have his own page recording the sale." I place the Thistlewood leaf on the arm of her chair, then add more gently, "And a second matter, if you'll allow it: your mother once took in a road-priest called Elowen Ashgrove, with a babe wrapped in green velvet. I think that babe grew up to sit before you."

input.add_to_description: Day 4 night: Read the Thistlewood ledger leaf, accepts the ford tale is forged (she half suspected). Remembers Elowen Ashgrove staying at the manor ~20 years ago with a baby (Maren then in her twenties). Her mother Lady Agnes kept the child three months. Then Corvin arrived with a "letter in Elowen's hand" (forged) asking for the child, and Lady Agnes, ill and believing it, gave the baby up and the key to a small iron coffer Elowen had left "for the girl when she is grown". Corvin took both. The coffer itself, bearing the Lantern sign and E.A., remains in the manor's strongroom, locked; its key went with Corvin. Maren lets Wren see it.

time: 30 minutes later: Day 4, 7:30 PM

She reads the leaf by the firelight, once, then again, her ink-stained thumb moving along Corvin's neat hand. When she looks up there isn't surprise in her face, only a deep weariness, as of a debt long expected. "I wondered," she says. "I'd sit under that painting and think, no man ever looked so tidy in a river." She folds the leaf and holds it as if it weighed a great deal. "The ford tale held for twenty years because no one dared look. Now the village will."

Then your second matter lands, and the weariness changes into something stranger. She is quiet for a long time. She looks at your face, your eyes, the way you hold your hands.

"I was twenty-four when she came," she says. "A road-priest, thin as a heron, with a baby in a blanket the colour of a forest. My mother was sick that year, and she took them in without a question. The child slept in my own old cradle by that fire for three months, until the road-priest went out one evening and didn't come back." Her voice catches. "Then a man arrived, a storyteller, charming, silver-tongued, with a letter in the priest's hand asking for the child to be given to him. My mother was ill and she believed it. She gave him the baby, and the key to a coffer the priest had left behind 'for the girl when she's grown.' I watched him ride away with her." She presses her lips together. "I've wondered for twenty years if I should have said something."

She rises. "The coffer is still here. Mother wouldn't send it away, and the key went with the storyteller. Come."

She leads you down a stair to a small stone strongroom, and by the light of her candle you see it on a shelf: a little iron-bound coffer scratched with a lantern and the letters *E.A.* It is no bigger than a bread-box. Locked.

You've heard Corvin's name linked to this twice in a day. He has the key, and he'll be at the ford at dusk tomorrow.

What does Wren do?

"Thank you, my lady. Twenty years is a long time to carry that, and I won't hold any of it against you." I set the candle on the shelf and kneel at the coffer, running a fingertip over the lantern scratches and the keyhole, then turn the brass reliquary over in my hand. "May I try something odd first? Elowen made this case and this coffer, and I wonder if the lantern's foot or the ring on its base is more than ornament. If it isn't, I'll ask you for a smith's fine awl and a steady hour, and I'll not force the lid."

time: 40 minutes later: Day 4, 8:10 PM

You kneel on the cold stones with the candle on the shelf above you and turn the little brass lantern in your hands. Your Investigation check was an 18. Under the base, hidden among the cast rays, a boss of metal stands a hair proud, and it isn't a decoration. It has teeth. It's a key.

You hold your breath and fit it to the coffer's keyhole. It slides in with a small, soft click, as if it had been waiting twenty years, and turns. Lady Maren catches her breath behind you. The iron key Corvin carried off was never going to fit.

The lid rises. Inside, on a bed of faded green velvet, lie three things: a small silver pendant shaped like a lantern, a folded paper sealed with plain wax and marked with a lamp-staff, and a single letter in a looped hand you know from the parchment in your reliquary. It's addressed on the outside: *To my wren.*

You read it kneeling, with a hand over your mouth. It isn't long. Elowen writes that Corvin Tallowmere was her own apprentice, that he turned her blessings into pedigrees and sold the road's mercy to men who wanted it for their vanity, and that she meant to confront him. If she did not return, she wrote, he would come for the child with false letters and a pleasant face. *Light the road, don't sell it. You'll know what that means when you're old enough to be ashamed.* Beneath the signature, a lantern with a crooked flame. The folded paper is a commission, naming you heir to her lamp-staff and her calling, if you want it.

You've gained the letter, the pendant, and the commission, and learned more than you came for. It's ten past eight on Day 4. Corvin is a day's wait away at the ford, and he knows it is true.

Lady Maren waits quietly, hand on the door. What does Wren do?

I fold the letter against my chest for a long moment, then wipe my face with my sleeve and put the pendant on. "My lady, may I ask for a bed, a pen, and a few hours alone with this? Tomorrow I'm going to meet the man who raised me, and I'd like to know what I'll say before I open my mouth."

You fold the letter against your chest for a long moment, wipe your face with your sleeve, and clasp the little silver lantern around your neck. Lady Maren says nothing at all. She only nods once, the way you might nod to a stranger on a long road, and leads you up a narrow stair to a small, clean guest room with a bed, a table, a pen, and a candle. She sets a jug of water and a heel of bread by your hand and withdraws, closing the door softly behind her.

Someone else shouts that the Thistlewoods should refund every penny. A tankard flies. Two of Lady Maren's men-at-arms, Alder and Kit by their badges, take you by the elbows and hustle you out the back as the room swells into a roar. Your voice carries clear across the water, and for a moment the whole ford holds still. On the bank the wagon halts, the painted lantern swinging on its side, and the brown-coated man looks up, then at the figure climbing down from the driving-box.

Corvin Tallowmere is exactly as you left him. He's a tall man in his fifties, silver-haired, in a good dark coat and ink-black gloves, with a face that always looks as though it's on the verge of being kind. He says something quiet to Garrow, who stops where he is with a glance at the willows, and then, alone, he steps onto the stones. He crosses with the unhurried grace of a man who has done it a thousand times, and he stops two stones from yours and spreads his gloved hands in the lamplight.

"Wren," he says, softly enough that only the water carries it beyond you. "You've grown. Even your scowl has grown." A rueful, warm smile. "You've been busy. I heard about Verrel, and about the common room. A wonderful speech, I'm told, if poorly received."

Your Insight check was a 12, and it isn't enough to tell you what's real in him. His voice is warm and level and sorry, and it gives you nothing at all. He tells you he never harmed Elowen Ashgrove. She walked away from him, he says, to travel the road alone, and he took the child to keep her safe. He says the blessings were only ever paper, but that he kept the faith in his own way. And then, so gently it's almost a kindness:

"She's alive, Wren. I know where. Give me the ledger, and I'll burn the Thistlewood and Dray pages with my own hands, make good what I can, and take you to her myself." The silver in his hair catches the last light. At his throat, on a cord, hangs a small iron key. "That's the whole bargain. A book for a mother."

Behind him on the bank, the driver has put a crossbow across his knees, and Garrow rests a hand on a short sword under his coat. Hob puffs at his pipe. Alder and Kit hold very still in the willows. The villagers murmur.

What does Wren say or do?

I keep my voice pitched to carry to the bank, and I smile at him without warmth. "Master Tallowmere, you've a crossbow across your driver's knees and a sword under Garrow's coat, which is a strange way to take a girl to meet her mother. Here's my bargain, so everyone on this bank can hear it: tell me her name and the town she's in, tonight, and the ledger stays sealed in Lady Maren's keeping until I've met her myself."

I lift Elowen's letter just enough for the lamplight to show the looped hand. "She wrote that you'd come for me with false letters and a pleasant face. So prove her wrong, Master, and name the town."

The ford is very quiet. Even the water seems to hush. Corvin's gaze lingers on the letter in your hand, on the looped hand you both know, and for the space of one breath his face loses all its warmth and becomes only a thing at rest, thoughtful and cold. Then the kindness comes back like a lamp being turned up.

"Saltmarsh," he says. "She's in Saltmarsh, below the keep on the estuary. You know I wouldn't lie about her." He says it just loud enough for the bank. "There, child. A town, as you asked." His gloved hand opens toward you, palm up. "Now the book. Tonight. Not in Lady Maren's keeping, not in anyone's keeping but mine, where it can be put right before it hurts the innocent."

You can't tell whether he's lying. It's the one thing he taught you that you never learned to see through from the outside.

Behind him there's a click, the crossbow being cocked, and the driver lifts it from his knees with its point just short of you. Garrow draws the short sword halfway from under his coat. On the near bank, two shapes step out of the willows, Alder and Kit with their spears levelled, and the villagers' murmur sharpens into a shout. Hob, at his green door, takes the pipe from his mouth.

Then, for the whole bank to hear, I add, "Everyone heard Master Tallowmere name Saltmarsh, so if anything happens to me, you all know exactly where to look for him."
