RULE Dropping to 0 Hit Points:
When you drop to 0 hit points, you either die outright or fall unconscious, as explained in the following sections.

#### Instant Death

Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 hit points and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.

For example, a cleric with a maximum of 12 hit points currently has 6 hit points. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to 0 hit points, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the cleric dies.

#### Falling Unconscious

If damage reduces you to 0 hit points and fails to kill you, you fall unconscious (see appendix PH-A). This unconsciousness ends if you regain any hit points.

#### Death Saving Throws

Whenever you start your turn with 0 hit points, you must make a special saving throw, called a death saving throw, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other saving throws, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by spells and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a saving throw.

Roll a d20. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any hit points or become stable.

***Rolling 1 or 20.*** When you make a death saving throw and roll a 1 on the d20, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the d20, you regain 1 hit point.

***Damage at 0 Hit Points.*** If you take any damage while you have 0 hit points, you suffer a death saving throw failure. If the damage is from a critical hit, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

#### Stabilizing a Creature

The best way to save a creature with 0 hit points is to heal it. If healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be stabilized so that it isn't killed by a failed death saving throw.

You can use your action to administer first aid to an unconscious creature and attempt to stabilize it, which requires a successful DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check.

A **stable** creature doesn't make death saving throws, even though it has 0 hit points, but it does remain unconscious. The creature stops being stable, and must start making death saving throws again, if it takes any damage. A stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

#### Monsters and Death

Most GMs have a monster die the instant it drops to 0 hit points, rather than having it fall unconscious and make death saving throws.

Mighty villains and special nonplayer characters are common exceptions; the GM might have them fall unconscious and follow the same rules as player characters.

time: 25 minutes later: Day 5, 5:48:24 PM

The rapier's point had barely touched his collar when Corvin's eyes flicked over your shoulder. Your Intimidation check was a 3, and the driver took no heed of it. You see Corvin's mouth begin to curve, and he says nothing. He doesn't give the order. The bolt strikes before you can turn.

It's a critical hit. Eleven points of damage drop you off the stone and into the cold ford, and the world goes grey at the edges. You hear shouting, the splash of boots, water in your ears. One bolt more flies past you and misses. Then Alder's spear goes wide, and Kit's finds the driver, and he folds beside Garrow in the shallows.

You lie at the bottom of the dark. Twice you hear Alder's voice and Hob's wheeze over you, hands pressing at your wound and failing, and Kit swearing in a language you don't know. You make your death saves in the dark, one ten, then a thirteen before it, and the next round something bright and fierce answers in you: a natural 20. You come up gasping into the lamplight with one hit point and a mouthful of river.

Corvin is gone. When you turn your head, the flat stone is empty, a wet footprint drying on it. One of the wagon's horses is missing from the picket line, and the dusk has swallowed him. The wagon stands on the bank with its painted lantern, abandoned, and the strongbox sits on its tailboard, still locked.

You are alive. It's nearly six now, on Day 5. You're at 1 hit point, 1 spell slot left, and 225 XP, 75 short of the next level. I gave you 50 XP for the fight. Garrow and the driver are dead, and the villagers are gathered quietly on the bank, looking at you with a different face than they wore at noon. Lady Maren is hurrying down from the spur.

Corvin said "Saltmarsh," and you still have the ledger in your psalter, two leaves for Thistlewood and Dray, and a night of rest ahead.

What does Wren do?

I let Alder and Kit haul me onto the bank, cough up half the river, and manage a croaky "Thank you, both, and you, Hob." Then I ask Lady Maren for a bed, and while I'm lying propped up I send Kit to search the driver's belt and pockets for the strongbox key, and Hob to keep an eye on the wagon until morning.

"In the morning," I add weakly, "I'm opening that strongbox, and then I'm riding for Saltmarsh."

Alder and Kit haul you up the bank like a netted fish, and you cough up what feels like half the Marrow. You manage a croaky "Thank you, both, and you, Hob," and Hob only snorts around his pipe, wiping his eyes with a knuckle. Lady Maren arrives at a run with a lantern and a blanket, takes one look at you, and says nothing at all for a moment. Then she orders a litter.

Before they carry you off, you send Kit to the driver, and he comes back with a dead man's belt-pouch. Inside is a small iron key, a few coppers, and a scrap of vellum folded small. Hob takes the wagon watch with a rug over his knees and his pipe, and Alder stays at his side.

You sleep in the same small room under the eaves, in a clean bed with a jug of water and a heel of bread. It's a long, heavy sleep, and when you wake the window is full of white morning. You're whole again: all your hit points and your spell slots, and Bardic Inspiration back at three. The night has passed without trouble.

At seven you go down to the yard with Kit. The wagon stands by the tithe-barn, its painted lantern faded in the daylight, and the strongbox sits on its tailboard. The little iron key fits. Inside, packed in straw, lie a good set of lock-picks and tools, a full forgery kit in a lacquered case, a purse of sixty gold pieces in mixed coin, and one slip of paper in Corvin's neat hand: *The Salt Gull, Saltmarsh, the ninth.*

That's Day 9. You've pocketed the money, the kit and the tools, and the note. The tools you wanted at the tinker's are now yours, 74 gold and some silver in all.

Lady Maren stands at your elbow, her hands clasped. "The village is quiet this morning," she says. "They saw you take a bolt for the truth. I think they'll listen now." She hesitates. "Will you ride for Saltmarsh? Sir Corwen Dray is a hard man, I hear, and proud. You'll want something to carry in front of you."

You have three days before the ninth. Saltmarsh is some five days' ride by the river road, so you won't make it by Day 9 without hard riding and a lucky road. You're at 225 XP, 75 short of level 2.

What does Wren do?

"I'll ride for Saltmarsh, my lady, and I'll have to ride hard to make the ninth." I tuck the thieves' tools and forgery kit into my pack, and for once I keep the forgery kit for honest work. "If you can spare a swift horse in place of Biscuit, and a letter under your own seal naming me your friend and Elowen Ashgrove's daughter, it'll open doors in Saltmarsh that Lord Edric's letter won't."

I turn to Kit with a grin. "And if Alder can spare you for a week, I'd gladly buy your spear on the road, a lady needs a second pair of eyes when she's chasing a man who nearly watched her die."

time: 45 minutes later: Day 6, 7:45:24 AM

Lady Maren doesn't answer at once. She looks at the wagon, at the faded lantern, at Alder leaning on his spear, and then at you. "A horse, yes. My father's grey, Ember, who's too good for this village and bored with it. And a letter." She goes into the manor and returns within a quarter of an hour with a sealed square of vellum, and she hands it over with both hands, as if it were heavier than it looked. She has written it in her own square hand, naming you her friend and Elowen Ashgrove's daughter, "with every claim on the house of Thistlewood that her mother had, and gladly given."

Biscuit goes back to the stable with the promise that Lord Edric's stable-boy will fetch him when the dust settles. Ember is a tall grey with a white blaze and an opinion of himself, and he regards you the way a cat regards a puddle.

Then she turns to Kit. "I'll not order it. I'll ask." Kit says nothing for a moment, one thumb in her sword-belt. She looks at the wagon, at the ford, at you. "Aye," she says at last. "I've never been past the weir. Time I saw where the river goes." Alder claps her on the shoulder, and Lady Maren pays her a month's wage in advance without being asked. Kit stows her shield on her back, shoulders a pack, and gives you a brief, dry nod, no speech.

Kit is a human fighter, a solid companion with chain mail, a shield, a longsword, a light crossbow and a steady head. She has her own character sheet now and takes her turns as herself in a fight, on your orders if you give them.

It's quarter to eight on Day 6. Saltmarsh is days away, and the Salt Gull meeting is on Day 9. The river road runs down past Marrowford and Thornhallow, and you can leave now, or stop on the way.

What does Wren do?

"Then let's ride, Kit. You take the first watch tonight and I'll take the second, and I'll teach you a song to pass the miles." I swing up onto Ember, who snorts at me in disdain, and pat his neck. "We'll stop at Thornhallow on the way, because I'd like to see how Dame Crowe judged the Verrels, and ask Lord Edric whether Tobin and Brother Osric are safe."

input.add_to_description: Day 7 at Thornhallow: Dame Crowe came Day 4, heard Lord Edric's confession and Osric's attestation. Ruling: the Aldermere precedence and tax-right are struck from the Verrel charter and a fine levied; the plain land-grant stands, so the manor is kept. Crowe wants Corvin Tallowmere and the ledger. time: 1 day 8 hours later: Day 7, 3:45:24 PM

Ember sulks for the first mile and then, as you sing, begins to keep time with his ears. Your Performance check was an 18. Kit says nothing through the first verse, hums the second under her breath, and by the third is bellowing the chorus flat and cheerful. You pass the night at Lantern's Rest, where Marta feeds you both and refuses payment, and ride on through Marrowford the next day.

You reach Thornhallow at a quarter to four on Day 7. The green and white pennant still flies. Tobin sees you from the gate and runs the whole courtyard, nearly knocking Kit over. Lord Edric meets you in the study with his shirt-sleeves rolled, and tells it quickly.

Dame Crowe came on the fourth day, at noon exactly. She heard his confession and Osric's sworn word and went through the register herself. Her ruling: the Aldermere line is struck from the charter, the precedence and tax-right are forfeit, and a fine is levied. But the land-grant is plain and old, and the manor stands. "I am still lord of Thornhallow," he says, wondering, "and I sleep." Hale is held for her court. Tobin and Osric are safe, and Osric has taken to reading the register aloud to anyone who stands still.

Crowe also left a message for you: she wants the storyteller Corvin Tallowmere, and the ledger, brought to her. She says a girl who confesses unprompted is worth hearing, and that she will be at the Marrowford assize at month's end.

The road to Saltmarsh runs on three days further, and the ninth is two days off. You and Kit have a night's bed here if you want it.

What does Wren do?

I take a hot meal and a few hours' sleep, but I tell Lord Edric we ride before dawn, since the ninth is two days off and the road to Saltmarsh is three. Before we go I ask him to keep Osric and Tobin close, and I give Tobin a quick hug and the silver lantern's blessing, a thumb pressed to his forehead.

input.add_to_description: Ledger leaf details (Day 7): betrothal tied Sir Corwen's heir, his daughter Isaude Dray, to the Vantry merchant-house of Saltmarsh (wool and salt trade). Written beside it: sum 140 marks paid, and a date, the ninth of the month, circled, "the wedding-contract to be sealed before witnesses." That is the same ninth as the Salt Gull note.

You eat, sleep a few hours, and Lord Edric keeps his word about Osric and Tobin without being asked twice. Before you go you press a thumb to Tobin's forehead and say the Lantern-Bearer's short blessing. He goes red to the ears and says nothing, which for Tobin is eloquent.

You take out the Dray leaf by the candle to check it again before the road. Corvin's neat hand: the betrothal ties Sir Corwen's daughter and heir, Isaude Dray, to the Vantry merchant-house of Saltmarsh, wool and salt. Beside it, 140 marks paid, and a date circled hard: the ninth, "the wedding-contract to be sealed before witnesses."

That's the same ninth as the note from the strongbox. Corvin isn't just meeting someone at the Salt Gull. The forged contract is to be sealed that day, and he plans to be there.

The rest has put you at full strength, with spells and Inspiration restored. It's near midnight now on Day 7. Two days remain, and the road is three. You'll need to ride hard, and likely through the night.

What does Wren do?

I roll the Dray leaf away and look at Kit. "Then we ride now, and we trade off dozing in the saddle. If the Vantry contract is sealed on the ninth, Corvin will be in the room, and I'd rather arrive with one tired horse than miss him by an hour."

I check Ember's girth, tie the saddlebags tight, and ask Kit to take the front for the first stretch while I hum the road song low to keep us both awake.

RULE Speed:
Every character and monster has a speed, which is the distance in feet that the character or monster can walk in 1 round. This number assumes short bursts of energetic movement in the midst of a life-threatening situation.

The following rules determine how far a character or monster can move in a minute, an hour, or a day.

#### Travel Pace

While traveling, a group of adventurers can move at a normal, fast, or slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace table. The table states how far the party can move in a period of time and whether the pace has any effect. A fast pace makes characters less perceptive, while a slow pace makes it possible to sneak around and to search an area more carefully.

***Forced March.*** The Travel Pace table assumes that characters travel for 8 hours in day. They can push on beyond that limit, at the risk of exhaustion.

For each additional hour of travel beyond 8 hours, the characters cover the distance shown in the Hour column for their pace, and each character must make a Constitution saving throw at the end of the hour. The DC is 10 + 1 for each hour past 8 hours. On a failed saving throw, a character suffers one level of exhaustion (see appendix PH-A).

***Mounts and Vehicles.*** For short spans of time (up to an hour), many animals move much faster than humanoids. A mounted character can ride at a gallop for about an hour, covering twice the usual distance for a fast pace. If fresh mounts are available every 8 to 10 miles, characters can cover larger distances at this pace, but this is very rare except in densely populated areas.

Characters in wagons, carriages, or other land vehicles choose a pace as normal. Characters in a waterborne vessel are limited to the speed of the vessel, and they don't suffer penalties for a fast pace or gain benefits from a slow pace. Depending on the vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to travel for up to 24 hours per day.

Certain special mounts, such as a pegasus or griffon, or special vehicles, such as a *carpet of flying*, allow you to travel more swiftly.

##### Travel Pace

| Pace   | Distance per: Minute | Hour    | Day      | Effect                                           |
|--------|----------------------|---------|----------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Fast   | 400 feet             | 4 miles | 30 miles | -5 penalty to passive Wisdom (Perception) scores |
| Normal | 300 feet             | 3 miles | 24 miles | -                                                |
| Slow   | 200 feet             | 2 miles | 18 miles | Able to use stealth                              |

#### Difficult Terrain

The travel speeds given in the Travel Pace table assume relatively simple terrain: roads, open plains, or clear dungeon corridors. But adventurers often face dense forests, deep swamps, rubble-filled ruins, steep mountains, and ice-covered ground-all considered difficult terrain.

You move at half speed in difficult terrain--moving 1 foot in difficult terrain costs 2 feet of speed-so you can cover only half the normal distance in a minute, an hour, or a day.

CONDITION Exhaustion:
Some special abilities and environmental hazards, such as starvation and the long-term effects of freezing or scorching temperatures, can lead to a special condition called exhaustion. Exhaustion is measured in six levels. An effect can give a creature one or more levels of exhaustion, as specified in the effect's description.
1 - Disadvantage on ability checks
2 - Speed halved
3 - Disadvantage on attack rolls and saving throws
4 - Hit point maximum halved

6 - Death
If an already exhausted creature suffers another effect that causes exhaustion, its current level of exhaustion increases by the amount specified in the effect's description.
A creature suffers the effect of its current level of exhaustion as well as all lower levels. For example, a creature suffering level 2 exhaustion has its speed halved and has disadvantage on ability checks.
An effect that removes exhaustion reduces its level as specified in the effect's description, with all exhaustion effects ending if a creature's exhaustion level is reduced below 1.
Finishing a long rest reduces a creature's exhaustion level by 1, provided that the creature has also ingested some food and drink.

You ride through the night with Kit in front and the road song humming between you. You are both at exhaustion level 2: disadvantage on ability checks, and speed halved. That's the rule, and it's why the last miles drag. You stop at a lock-keeper's cottage in the afternoon for a few hours' sleep and some bread, then limp on through Day 8's evening and dawn along the widening river as the air turns to salt and gull-cry.

It's a quarter to ten on the morning of the ninth. Saltmarsh spreads below you on a grey estuary: slate roofs, drying nets, a stone quay, the squat bulk of Saltmarsh Keep on a rise to the north. Banners of white and blue hang from the keep. In the town below, a bell has begun to toll the hour, and a small crowd is moving toward a hall by the quay marked with the Vantry scales.

You hand Ember to a quay-boy with a copper, and Kit tucks her shield across her back under a cloak. The Salt Gull is low and tarred, smelling of fish, smoke and wet rope. You take the corner table with sightlines to the stair and the door, and order two bowls of chowder, which costs a silver piece.

Then you lean on the bar and ask your question, soft and friendly. Your Persuasion check was an 8 with disadvantage from exhaustion. The innkeeper, Bess Harl, a broad wary woman with scarred forearms, doesn't bite. "No storyteller here, love," she says, much too quickly. But her eyes touched the stair first, and then a door at the top of it, closed, with a new brass lock.

You eat, slowly. Kit sits with her back to the wall and her eyes on the stair. Down the quay the bell has stopped tolling, and the crowd has gone into the Vantry hall. The contract sealing will be happening in there, perhaps within the hour.

At a quarter past ten, a man in good black gloves comes down the stairs from that locked room, carrying a leather case under his arm. He's not Corvin. He's younger, tidy, with ink on his cuffs, and he doesn't see you. He heads out toward the Vantry hall at a quick walk.

What does Wren do?

I murmur to Kit, "Follow the clerk with the case and don't lose him, and if he reaches the Vantry hall, get close and listen." Then I finish my chowder, pay Bess with a warm smile, and drift up the stair as if I were looking for the privy, kneel at the new brass lock on the closed door with my thieves' tools, and set to work as quietly as I can.

Kit rises with a dry nod and goes out after the clerk. Chain mail and a tired step make a poor shadow, though. Her Stealth was a 7, and at the turn of the quay the young man glances back, sees a stocky woman in a blue tabard, and picks up his pace toward the Vantry hall's wide doors.

You pay Bess with a smile and drift up the stair. The brass lock is new and good. Your Dexterity check was a 9, with disadvantage from exhaustion and no proficiency with the tools. The pick skids off the pin. A heavy tread comes up behind you, and Bess Harl stands on the landing with her scarred arms folded.

"I don't know what you think you're doing, mistress," she says quietly, "but that lock is paid for through the ninth, and the man who paid had a crossbow in his bag and a way of saying please." She doesn't raise her voice. "Be on your way, and I'll say nothing to the watch."

Below, through the window, you can see the Vantry hall's doors, and Kit standing at the edge of the crowd, looking back toward you.

What does Wren do?

I pocket the pick, lower my voice, and meet Bess's eye plainly. "Then I'll be honest, since you've no reason to like me: the man in that room sells forged pedigrees, and a wedding contract of his will be sealed in the Vantry hall within the hour, a lie that will ruin two families. I carry a letter under Lady Maren Thistlewood's seal, and here are ten gold pieces for one favour, which is to tell me whether he's in that room right now, and how many are with him."

input.add_to_description: Day 9: Bess Harl refused Wren's gold (Persuasion 9). She says the man in the room keeps her inn afloat and has paid for her silence; she will not say who is inside. She is frightened, not loyal. She did say, grimly, that "the wedding folk at the hall will be done by noon."

You keep your voice low and plain, and you lay the Thistlewood letter in her hand with the coins beside it. Bess reads the seal, and for a breath something moves behind her eyes. Your Persuasion check was a 9 with disadvantage, and it isn't enough.

She pushes the gold back at you without counting it. "No." The word is quiet and tired. "He pays for this roof, and for my silence, and he's a man who remembers who talks. I'll not say who's in that room or how many." She hesitates, then adds, grimly, almost against her will, "I'll say the wedding folk at the hall will be done by noon. After that I can't say what comes down my stair."

She isn't a villain. She's frightened, and she's given you the one thing she can: the hour. It's twenty past ten. At noon the contract is sealed, and whoever is behind the brass lock has until then to be somewhere else.

Down on the quay, Kit is a blue spot at the edge of the crowd before the Vantry hall. The clerk with the case has gone inside.

What does Wren do?

I scoop the coins back with a nod of thanks and leave Bess be, then slip into the alley by the stairs and cast Disguise Self, making myself a tidy, ink-stained notary's junior with a wax-tablet satchel and a sober face. I catch Kit's eye outside the Vantry hall, murmur, "You're my escort from the guildhouse, so look bored and stern," and walk us both straight through the doors as if we were late.

Inside I hold the Dray leaf ready under the psalter and find a place near the sealing table to see who holds the contract.

Behind the alley wall you make the quick gestures and the Lantern-Bearer's small trick takes hold. Your face thins and pales, ink blooms on your fingers, and a wax-tablet satchel hangs from your shoulder. One spell slot spent, and the disguise holds for an hour. You catch Kit's eye and murmur the plan, and she gives a bored, stern look that is no act at all.

The door is another matter. Your Deception check was a 7 with disadvantage, and the doorman, a stout man in Vantry grey with a ledger of his own, isn't fooled by a story, only unconvinced by a notary's junior who has no token. "Which guildhouse? Whose warrant? Mine says all notaries were seated at nine." He doesn't doubt your face, just your paperwork. "No token, no entry. Come back with the master."

You're not unmasked, and you've still got the hour. Kit, who has the better eyes, tips her head very slightly. Along the hall's flank, past a stack of salt-barrels, is a small side door propped on a brick, and through it a clerk with a tray of inkpots is moving in. Voices carry out of the high windows, a dry formal cadence: the reading of terms. It's half past ten, and you've fifty minutes of disguise.

What does Wren do?

I give the doorman a prim little nod, say "Then I'll fetch the master," and walk Kit round the corner past the salt-barrels. At the propped side door I lift a spare tray of ink-pots from the stack by the wall, hold it like it belongs to me, and slip in behind the other clerk with Kit a pace behind as my "escort," eyes down and mouth shut.

You set the tray down with a small clatter, and the murmur of the hall dips. You step into the open before the dais and say it clearly, as you rehearsed on the road. Your Persuasion check was an 18, even with the weight of exhaustion on you, and it lands.

The hall is long and cool, with scales carved above the dais and salt-white light from the high windows. Behind a table sit four figures. Sir Corwen Dray is a grey, upright man with a hard jaw and a harder stare. Beside him is his daughter Isaude, a pale girl of perhaps eighteen, gripping the arm of her chair. Opposite them are the Vantry elder, stout and cautious, and his son, the intended groom, who looks mostly relieved to be spoken to. At the table's end sits the arbiter, a thin woman in grey with a stylus behind her ear. Beside the contract case stands the young clerk in black gloves, and his face has gone very still.

"Who are you?" Sir Corwen says. "And what page?"

The arbiter raises a hand before you can answer. "Hold, Sir Corwen. A seal set on a doubted paper cannot be unset. Let the notary's junior show what she has. Briefly." She glances at the water-clock. "The hour is not yet noon."

Your Disguise Self has forty minutes left. Kit stands at the wall by the side door, hand easy on her belt. The clerk in black hasn't moved, but his eyes have gone to the door on the far side of the dais, which stands slightly ajar. Someone may be listening behind it.

You hold the leaf up with your thumb over the initial and say it plainly. For a breath the hall is so quiet you can hear the water-clock dripping.

Your Persuasion check was a 9 with disadvantage, and it doesn't carry. Sir Corwen is on his feet before you finish, his chair scraping. "A forger's account-book? Brought by a notary's junior no one here has seated?" He turns on the arbiter. "Madam, you have just heard my daughter's name and my coin called a swindle by a stranger with no token."

The arbiter doesn't answer him. She holds out a thin, ink-stained hand. "The page, then. And your name, and your guildhouse." Her voice is level, but the stylus has come down from behind her ear. "A seal can wait until noon. A slander cannot be unsaid."

The young clerk in black gloves has slid two steps toward the far door. He stops when your head turns.

Then the door swings open the rest of the way, and Corvin Tallowmere walks through it.

He looks as he always did, silver hair combed back and black gloves, as unhurried as a man entering his own parlour. There's a smear of river mud on one boot, and nothing else. He doesn't look at the arbiter or at Sir Corwen. He looks at you, past the ink on your fingers and the notary's thin face, and smiles his gentle teacher's smile.

"Hello, Wren," he says warmly. "You've ridden hard. You look dreadful."

Sir Corwen's head snaps round. The Vantry elder half rises. Across the hall, Kit's hand has gone still on her belt. Your disguise has thirty-eight minutes left, and it hasn't fooled the one man you most needed it to fool.

"Honored arbiter," Corvin says, still looking at you, "that page is mine. Stolen, along with the book it was cut from, by this girl, my runaway apprentice. I think she'd like very much to hand it over. Wouldn't you, my dear?"

What does Wren do?

I let the disguise stay and give Corvin a bright, sharp grin. "Thank you, Master Tallowmere, for confirming it's yours." I turn to the arbiter and hold the leaf higher. "He's just sworn before this hall that this page is his work. It records 140 marks paid for a betrothal tale, so ask him why a storyteller has a receipt for a contract that's about to be sealed as true."

transcript.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

Your grin is bright and your voice carries to the back of the hall. Your Persuasion check was a 16, even with exhaustion dragging at you, and it lands.

"Thank you, Master Tallowmere, for confirming it's yours."

The smile on Corvin's face doesn't move, but something behind it stops. He has just done the one thing he never lets a mark do, which is hand over the thread himself.

The arbiter's stylus is already in her fingers. "Master Tallowmere," she says, very evenly. "You say this page is yours. Then whose is the sum of one hundred and forty marks written upon it, and why does a storyteller keep a receipt for a betrothal that is to be sealed as true in this hall within the hour?"

Sir Corwen has gone grey around the mouth. He doesn't look at Corvin. He looks at his daughter. Isaude is staring at the page in your hand with her lips parted, and you realise she has understood it before her father has.

"My lady arbiter," Corvin begins, lightly, a man starting a story. "A tale-teller's trade is..."

"I did not ask for a trade," she says. "I asked for an answer."

The Vantry elder is whispering furiously to his son. The clerk in black gloves has gone white and is edging toward the side of the dais, his case clutched to his chest. At the wall, Kit has taken one slow step off the brick and now stands between him and the way out.

Corvin's gaze slides to you at last, and his voice drops so that only the front of the room can hear it. "You haven't thought this through, my dear. If I'm a forger, then so is the girl who holds my ledger. Shall we tell them how you came by it?" He lets that sit. "Or shall you and I step into the back room and settle it like family?"

The arbiter hasn't looked away from him. "The seal stays unset," she says. "Sir Corwen, sit. The page, mistress."

She is holding out her hand for it. Your disguise has thirty-six minutes left.

What does Wren do?

I end the disguise with a flick of my fingers so my own face shows, hand the Dray leaf into the arbiter's palm, and meet her eyes. "My name is Wren Ashgrove, madam, and he's right about one thing: I took his ledger, and I'm not ashamed of it. I took it from the man who sold the nobles' pedigrees so I could return the truth to the houses he cheated."

I nod at the letters in my satchel. "I carry a letter from Lady Maren Thistlewood, a ruling from Dame Ilsabet Crowe's court that wants Corvin Tallowmere brought before her, and a register from Brother Osric, and I'll lay them all before you gladly."

transcript.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

You flick two fingers, and the notary's thin face melts away. The ink fades from your hands. There's a stir along the benches, and a small, startled sound from Isaude Dray. Your own face looks back at the hall, a half-elf girl, travel-stained and grey with weariness, but unhidden. The spell is ended by your action and costs nothing more.

You lay the Dray leaf in the arbiter's palm. "My name is Wren Ashgrove, madam. He's right about one thing: I took his ledger, and I'm not ashamed of it."

You set the rest of it on the table in a neat row: Lady Maren's letter under the Thistlewood seal, Lord Edric Verrel's letter vouching for you, and Brother Osric's copied register entry. The arbiter reads the leaf first. Her eyes move down it once, fast, then slowly. Then she breaks the Thistlewood wax with a thumbnail and reads that. When she gets to the line about Elowen Ashgrove's daughter, she looks up at you for a moment.

"A letter from Lord Edric, which names Dame Crowe," she says. "I see a lord's letter and a lady's. I do not see a ruling in Dame Crowe's hand." She says it without heat, a clerk noting a gap. "You'll want to be careful what you call a ruling in this hall, mistress. But the page..." She turns the leaf to Sir Corwen. "Is that your sum, sir?"

Sir Corwen takes the leaf in a hand that isn't steady. He reads it, and the hard jaw works once. "A hundred and forty marks," he says hoarsely. "Paid to a man at Ashby Weir three winters gone, for a tale of our house. I was told it was a copy of an old charter, only a copy." He lowers the page. "Isaude."

"Father," Isaude says. Her voice is small and clear. "I never met a Dray who needed a storyteller to be one. I'd rather be married on the truth than on that."

The Vantry elder has gone very quiet, and so has his son, who looks at Isaude with an expression that might be gratitude.

The arbiter lifts her stylus. "The sealing is stayed until the contract has been read against the keep's own rolls," she says. "Hall guard!" Two men in Vantry grey straighten at the main doors.

But Corvin is no longer in the middle of the room. While every eye was on the page, he has drifted back along the dais toward the open door behind it, one gloved hand resting lightly on the frame. The young clerk has seized the moment too, and is sidling after him, case hugged to his chest. Corvin's eyes meet yours across the hall, with no smile at all now.

"A pleasant morning's work, my dear," he says, very softly. "Remember I offered."

He is two steps from the door, with the guards still forty feet off and Kit at the far wall. What does Wren do?

"Kit, the clerk and his case!" I shout, already running along the dais, and I raise my voice to the hall. "Hall guard, the back door, Tallowmere is leaving!" Then I cast Mage Hand and send the pale hand snatching at the latch to swing the door shut in Corvin's face, while I vault the low step to block his way.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

"Kit, the clerk and his case! Hall guard, the back door!"

Your voice cracks across the hall like a whip, and everything happens at once. Kit is moving before you finish, and she is slower than usual, since exhaustion has halved her stride as it has yours. But she doesn't need speed. The clerk has been sidling along the dais with his case hugged to his chest, and when he sees a stocky woman in a blue tabard bearing down on him he stops dead, as a rabbit does under a hawk.

You flick two fingers and a pale, shimmering hand appears by the doorframe. Mage Hand doesn't need to hit anything. It only has to push, and the door isn't locked. It swings shut in Corvin's face with a solid wooden thud, just as his gloved fingers close on the latch ring.

Then you run. With your speed halved by exhaustion it's a stiff, graceless run, but you take the low step in a clumsy hop and land at the dais's edge, five feet short of him, breathing hard. That is as far as you can get this turn. It's close enough.

Corvin stands with his hand still on the latch and his back to you. For a moment his shoulders do nothing at all. Then he turns, and the gentle teacher's mask is gone, and what's under it is only a tired, cold, calculating man.

"That was clever," he says, quietly enough that the hall can't hear. "I taught you the hand."

Behind you, the two Vantry guards are crossing the floor at a steady jog, halberds up, and the arbiter's voice rings out: "Hold that man!" Kit has the clerk by the sleeve, and the case has fallen on the floor with a clack of metal fittings. Sir Corwen is on his feet, and Isaude has stood with him.

Corvin's eyes flick to the door, then to the guards, then back to you. The latch ring is under his hand, and he could try to haul it open again. One look says he is weighing it.

The guards will reach him in about three heartbeats. You've a rapier at your hip, a dagger, one spell slot, and a few seconds. What does Wren do?

"Corvin," I say, low and steady, and cast Charm Person on him with my last slot, keeping my tone as warm as his own once was. "You said you'd take me to my mother, so tell me honestly, just you and me, where she is. Stay with me until the guards come, and I'll speak for you at Dame Crowe's court."

transcript.result: added to Corvin Tallowmere's description

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

You say it low, in the warm voice he taught you, and the last of your Lantern-Bearer's small magic goes out of you with a flick of the fingers. It leaves the slot spent.

It doesn't take. Corvin's eyes narrow a fraction, and he gives a short, rueful breath through his nose, like a man who has felt a pickpocket's fingers and decided to be amused. "Oh, my dear," he says. "That was *mine*. I taught you to reach for the heart first. A mark has to want to be reached."

He doesn't bolt. The guards are on him, two halberds crossing in front of his chest and a heavy hand on each arm. He lets them take him with the grace of a man who has been arrested before. His gloves stay folded and his chin stays up.

"I'll answer your question, Wren," he says, so quietly the guards can't hear it, "but not here, and not with ears. Come and ask me once you've decided what you are." He smiles then, a thin one. "You've not yet decided. I can see it."

The arbiter's voice rings out behind you. "He is held in the hall's cellar under the guard's key until Sir Corwen's reeve and the keep's justice have the contract read against the rolls. Nobody speaks to him but by my leave." She looks at you. "Including you, mistress. I'll hear your case in full this afternoon, with that book of yours."

Kit comes up beside you with the clerk firmly by the collar. He has gone grey and he's babbling already: *he only copied, he was paid by the Dray steward, there are two more copies in the case.* She sets the leather case in your hands. It's heavy, with a brass catch.

Sir Corwen crosses the dais and stops in front of you. He looks old suddenly. "Girl," he says. "You've cost me a hundred and forty marks and a good name." He pauses, and his jaw works. "And you've saved my daughter from a worse bargain. I don't know which of those I'm to be angry about." Isaude comes and stands beside him, and she gives you a small, shy nod.

It is a quarter to eleven. Your disguise is gone and your spell slots are empty. Corvin is under lock and key, the ledger leaf is in the arbiter's hands, and you still owe the hall your account at noon. A man you once called master said you haven't decided what you are, and he has a word to say about your mother.

What does Wren do?

I take a long breath and speak to Sir Corwen and the arbiter together. "I'll give the hall my full account at noon, ledger and all, and swear it before the Lantern-Bearer, but first may I sit down, drink something, and sleep two hours? I'm half-dead on my feet, and I'd like to be clear-headed when I speak against a man like Corvin."

Then, quieter, to Kit: "Guard that case with your life. And afterward I want to speak to Corvin in the cellar, with the arbiter's leave, because whatever he knows about my mother, he won't say it to anyone else."

transcript.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

The arbiter considers you over the rim of her spectacles. A girl swaying on her feet isn't much of a witness, and she knows it. "Sit, drink, sleep," she says. "I will hear you at two bells past noon, in this hall, with the ledger and your oath. The elder will lend you his counting-room." She glances at the leather case in Kit's arms. "That stays under your companion's hand and my seal. I'll have it counted when you wake." She gives a dry nod. "As for the cellar, you may have a quarter hour with the prisoner after you've spoken, with a guard at the door. Not before."

It isn't what you asked for, but it's fair. The Vantry elder's son shows you to a small room off the hall, with a long table, a bench, and a window onto the quay. Someone brings bread, cold fish and a jug of small beer. You eat half of it standing. Kit takes the chair across the door, with the case on her knees and her longsword across it, and says nothing, which is what you'd have wanted from her anyway.

You sleep like a dropped stone. It's a short rest only, and you wake stiff, still hollow-eyed and heavy-limbed, with your spell slots still empty and the exhaustion still on you. A long rest will mend that, not a nap. Bardic Inspiration stands at three.

It is almost one in the afternoon. Gulls are crying on the quay. Kit hasn't moved, but a folded scrap of paper is lying on the table by your elbow, with no one near who could have put it there but the elder's son, who has gone. In a small, hurried hand: *The cellar guard says the prisoner has asked for you by name, and for no one else. He says to tell you "it was never the ledger." Isaude Dray*.

The hearing is at two. What does Wren do?

I read the note twice, fold it into the psalter, and look at Kit. "Whatever 'it was never the ledger' means, I'd rather decide with a clear head. Take me to the arbiter. I'll ask her to let me see Corvin for a few minutes now, with a guard at the door and you beside me, since he's asked for me and nobody else."

You accept the ruling with a small bow, and the arbiter's pen goes back to scratching. At a quiet bench by the wall, with Kit's shoulder to the room, you break the seal on Elowen's commission-paper.

It's one sheet in a firm, tilted hand, with the crooked-flame lantern pressed into the wax. It reads, in short plain lines: *I, Elowen Ashgrove, road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer, name my daughter Wren heir to my lamp-staff. It is in the keeping of the keeper of the Wick-House on the quay at Saltmarsh. Give it to the bearer of this paper who can also show the lantern-foot of my reliquary. Let no one else carry it.* Beneath, smaller: *Corvin Tallowmere knows where it is. He has never dared ask for it.*

So there's a shrine you can report to, the Wick-House, here in Saltmarsh, just down the quay. And Corvin has known all along where your mother's staff lay, and for twenty years he hasn't touched it. Whatever *it was never the ledger* means, it may start there.

You fold the paper away and spend the rest of the hour as you promised, laying out your account: ledger leaves first, then Osric's register, then Elowen's letter, murmuring it over to Kit in a low voice. She listens with her arms folded. When you finish, she grunts. "You say you took the book. They'll ask why you kept it two weeks and didn't burn it." After a moment she adds, "Tell them straight." It's the longest speech you've had from her all day. The rehearsal helps, and I rule it gives you advantage on the speaking check at the hearing.

At two the hall is full. The arbiter sits behind the dais table with the Dray leaf and the clerk's case before her. Sir Corwen and Isaude sit to one side, the Vantry elder and his son to the other. A guard stands at the cellar door at the back. Every eye in the room is on you.

"Wren Ashgrove," the arbiter says. "Speak."

What does Wren say?

I stand, set the psalter on the table, and speak plainly, not performing. "My name is Wren Ashgrove. I was raised by Corvin Tallowmere, and for nineteen years I helped him tell tales for money, until I found his ledger of forged pedigrees, sold to three houses, and I took it and ran."

I take the Verrel and Thistlewood outcomes in order, and I admit what I kept: "I kept the ledger for two weeks because I didn't know who to trust with it, and because I wanted to see for myself whether he'd harmed the houses or only flattered them." I slide the last leaf and the commission-paper into view. "I'm not asking you to forgive me, only to read what's written, and let Dame Crowe's court and Sir Corwen's keep decide what's true."

Level 2 is done. Wren has 17 hit points and three 1st-level slots, with Jack of All Trades, Song of Rest (d6), and Faerie Fire added to your spells. Kit levels up too. She shrugs, says "Take the steady number, I'm not one for dice," and goes to 20 hit points and gains Action Surge. Your slots are still empty until you rest properly.

The cellar steps are damp and narrow. A guard unlocks the heavy door, leans on the frame with his halberd, and gives you a look that says he'll hear every word. Kit stays on the stair behind you. Corvin sits on a barrel in the lamplight, hands folded, gloves on, as comfortable as a man at a patron's table.

"Thank you for coming," he says. "I'd hoped you'd be foolish enough to."

You ask him straight where your mother is. He doesn't answer at once. When he does, it's gentle. "I don't know, Wren. I swear that on the lantern I never believed in." He looks at his gloves. "Elowen was my teacher before I was yours. I turned her blessings into coin, and she knew it. The last time I saw her she was at Ashby Weir, alive and furious, with you in her arms. In the spring I came back for her and found the coffer, her key, and a lamp-mark on a stranger's wall. I never found her."

You watch his face as hard as a tired girl can. Your Insight check was a 5 with exhaustion, against a liar who taught you everything you know. You can't tell if he's lying. He tells it perfectly.

"As for 'it was never the ledger,'" he goes on, "I let you run with it. I let you keep it, and I left you notes to follow. The ledger was only a leash that pulled you in the right direction. There's a staff at the Wick-House that no one but Elowen's heir may take, and the keeper there showed me the door. I needed you here, with the lantern-foot and the paper." His eyes come up, quite steady. "Take me with you to the Wick-House, and I'll tell you everything I know about where she went. Leave me here and you'll learn it by guessing."

The guard shifts at the door. By your reckoning you've a few minutes left of the quarter hour.

What does Wren do?

"No, Corvin, you don't come with me." I stand and keep my voice flat. "You used me as a leash-dog for a staff you were too much of a coward to claim, and now you want a free walk to the Wick-House. Here's the trade: you tell the guard everything you know about Elowen, names, towns and dates, in writing, tonight, and I'll carry it to Dame Crowe's assize myself and say you helped. Refuse, and I find her without you."

I glance at the guard. "And I'd ask you to write it down word for word, friend, so he can't say later that I put words in his mouth."

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

Corvin's hands stay folded, but his eyes follow you up as you stand. For a moment the gentle teacher's face slips and he looks merely tired, and older than you remember.

"A leash-dog," he says. "Yes. That's fair." He doesn't argue it. "Writing, then. You've learned something, anyway. Paper that outlives the man is the only honest thing I ever sold."

He turns to the guard. "Friend, fetch ink and a clerk's hand, if you've a mind to be thorough. I'll dictate, and she may have her word for word." The guard looks at you, and you nod. He grunts and calls up the stair.

While he waits, Corvin lowers his voice, so only you hear it. "I'll put the towns and dates in it, and it will be true as far as I know it. But hear this part now, because it won't go in the writing. I wasn't the only one who knew about the staff, Wren. Someone else has come asking at the Wick-House since I did. A man who smiles a good deal." He holds your eyes. "You may remember the type. He'll be watching the quay by now. I'll name him when the statement is signed, not before."

The cellar clerk arrives with a lap-desk, and the guard gives you a tight nod. The quarter hour is done.

Upstairs the afternoon is wearing on. It's a little past three. Your spell slots are down to one of your three, and the exhaustion still sits on you like wet wool. The Wick-House is down the quay, and someone who smiles may be watching it. The Salt Gull's brass-locked room is also still unsearched, though Corvin is no longer paying for it.

What does Wren do?

I wait while the clerk's pen scratches Corvin's first lines, then step out and ask the arbiter for a hall guard and a warrant-word to open the brass-locked room at the Salt Gull, since Corvin's lease is as good as void now and Bess Harl will have cover to hand over the key. Kit and I will search it, take a room there for the night so we can finally do a proper long rest, and leave the Wick-House until dawn, when I can watch the quay first for a man who smiles too much.

Your Persuasion check was a 13 with disadvantage, and it's enough. The arbiter hardly looks up from Corvin's clerk. "Corvin's lease is forfeit with his goods," she says, "and a Vantry guard may stand where a magistrate cannot." She scrawls a warrant-word on a slip and hands you a broad, bored man named Pell with a halberd.

At the Salt Gull, Bess Harl reads the slip, the guard, and Kit's face. She unlocks the brass lock without a word, and her shoulders drop as if she'd been holding a heavy thing for days. "Take it," she mutters. "I'll be glad of the room back."

The room is bare of any person. Kit takes the door. You search with your Investigation check at an 8, which isn't a lot for tired eyes. You find a light crossbow with a bolt in it, a travelling bag with black gloves and spare shirts, a cold hearth, and in the ash a scrap of half-burned paper. It bears a crooked-flame lantern and a single word: *Wick*. That's your mother's mark. The rest of the room gives you nothing, though the boards under the bed feel loose to the boot. You can't be sure you've looked everywhere.

You take a room across the landing for five silver, with a bed for each of you and a bolt on the door. Pell goes back to the hall. It's nearly four, and you have the evening, a chance for a proper long rest, and the Wick-House waiting at dawn.

What does Wren do?

I kneel at the loose boards under the bed and lift them with my dagger tip, since this is a room where a man who hides things would hide one more. If there's anything underneath, I'll check it for traps before I touch it, with Kit watching the door.

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Salt Gull

You kneel and work the dagger tip under the board, and it comes up with a dry creak. Your Investigation check to look for a trap was a 6 with disadvantage, so you see nothing wrong. Corvin was always fond of cheap, nasty tricks.

As you reach in, a thread you never saw snaps taut. A stoppered ink-vial under the packet tips and bursts upward. You throw yourself sideways, and your Dexterity save was a 14, which beats the trap's DC 12. The ink splashes the floorboards and the underside of the bed, and spares your hands, face and the papers. Kit has turned from the door, one hand on her sword. She looks at the black stain, then at you, and says dryly, "He would."

Inside the cavity lies a small oilcloth packet, bone dry. In it you find:

A hand-drawn map of Saltmarsh's quay, in Corvin's neat hand, with the Salt Gull, the Vantry hall, and a small old building near the seaward end circled in red and labelled *Wick*. Three keys on a ring, one brass, one iron and one tiny and bent. And a folded note, also his: *The keeper sleeps till dawn bell. H. watches the east door.*

So the Wick-House keeper is asleep until dawn, and an "H." is watching one door of it, and Corvin had a plan to get in through some other. It's a little after four. The packet is yours now, unless you'd rather give it to the arbiter first.

You've a bed, a bolt on the door and a long evening before you. What does Wren do?

I wipe the ink off my boots, pocket the map, keys and note, and say, "H.? That can't be Hale, he's in a cellar in Thornhallow." I decide to keep the packet for now and show it to the arbiter only after I've seen the Wick-House myself, since an "H." who watches doors might also have friends in the hall.

Then I bolt the door, put Kit on the first watch, eat a hot supper sent up by Bess, and take my long rest, planning to be at the quay before the dawn bell.

The Salt Gull settles into its night noises of creaking beams, a drunk singing on the quay, and the slap of the tide. You wipe the ink off your boots, pocket the map, the keys and the note, and say what you think of "H." Kit only grunts. "Hale's got more than one hand," she says, which is more sense than you were ready for. You bolt the door. Bess herself sends up hot supper: eel pie, bread, and a warning that the east stair creaks. Kit takes the first watch, with her sword across her knees.

You sleep, and the night is quiet. You wake in the black before dawn, feeling like yourself again. The long rest has given back your hit points, your three spell slots and your Bardic Inspiration, and it has lifted exhaustion by one level, so you now carry level 1. That means disadvantage on ability checks still, but your speed is whole again. Kit is the same.

It is about four in the morning. The dawn bell is a couple of hours off, and the keeper of the Wick-House sleeps until it. The quay below is dark, damp, and mostly empty, with one lamp at the Vantry hall and fog off the estuary. You have the map, the keys, and the note that says an H. watches the east door.

What does Wren do?

I take Kit's arm and murmur, "Fog and darkness suit us. Leave your shield strapped and walk soft." We slip out the Salt Gull's back door and along the quay, where my darkvision lets me pick my way without a lamp, and I stop thirty paces from the Wick-House to study it against the map: which door is the east door, where a watcher would stand, and which way Corvin meant to get in. Then I put Kit at the corner of the lane with her crossbow ready and creep forward alone to look, keeping low in the fog.

The Wick-House sits near the seaward end of the quay, a squat old building of black timber and whitewashed stone, with a small lantern-shaped lamp, unlit, above a low door at the front. By the map, the east door is a narrow side entrance in the lane along its flank. Corvin's cross marks a third spot, a shuttered window at the back, above the tide-line.

Your Perception check was a 16 even with disadvantage, so you spot him before he spots you. He is half in shadow and half in the grey, and from a distance he looks like he is smiling.

Your Stealth check was only a 7, with disadvantage from exhaustion. A loose pebble turns under your boot, and the smiling man's head comes round at once. He doesn't start or reach for a weapon. He straightens, unhurried, and inclines his head across the fog like a servant greeting a guest.

The woman holding the candle is thin and stooped, with ink-stained fingers and sharp grey eyes. "Ysolde Vane," she says. "Keeper here thirty years. Your mother left a thing in my keeping, and I've turned away two men who wanted it, one with a kind voice and one with a smile."

She takes the commission-paper and reads it in the candle, then takes the reliquary. She doesn't ask for proof twice. From behind the altar she brings a staff of pale ash wood, as long as you are tall, with a brass lantern at its head. The crooked flame and *E.A.* are cut into the metal. She sets the reliquary's foot in a socket at the lantern's base and turns it. Something clicks, and the lantern's glass pane swings open on a hinge you never saw.

Inside, rolled thin as a cigarette, is a strip of paper in your mother's tilted hand: *I go to the Gullspit light. If I am not back by midwinter, light the road, not sell it. Trust the lamp, not the smile.*

"That's all she left," Ysolde says quietly, "except that I was to give the staff to you and no one else." She looks at you for a long moment. "You have her chin."

The staff is yours, with the strip of paper. The Gullspit light is a name you don't know. Outside, the fog is greying toward dawn, and the dawn bell will ring in perhaps an hour. Sparrow is still standing in the lane under Kit's crossbow.

I hold the staff for a moment, steadying my hand on the pale wood, then ask Mother Ysolde, "Do you know where the Gullspit light is, and who keeps it? And the man outside: could the shrine's wardens hold him for the dawn bell, or should I just let him walk and follow him back to his master?"

Exhaustion 1 only gives you disadvantage on ability checks, so your attack rolls and saves are clean. Kit is rested and unhurt too, with Second Wind and Action Surge ready.

Now the story. Mother Ysolde turns the lantern-foot over in her fingers and answers in her dry voice. "The Gullspit light is a stone beacon on the shingle spit across the estuary. It's been dark these fifteen years, since the channel moved and the ships stopped coming. It's three hours by the shore path at low tide, or one by boat. RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

Your Vicious Mockery hit Bandit 3 with a 13 on his save, exactly the DC, and he shrugged it off. Kit didn't need it. Her first swing took him for 9 and left him at the edge. She spent Action Surge, and her second swing missed. Then she snatched your last Bardic Inspiration die, rolled a 6, and turned the miss into a hit. The blade went through him, and the third hand fell across his friends on the threshold. Faerie Fire gutters out with the fight. You get 75 XP for the three bandits, so you're at 375 of 900.

You have no spell slots and no Inspiration left. Kit is at 15 of 20, with no Second Wind or Action Surge.

Then a shout comes from the lantern-room above, cracked with joy. "It's moving, it's moving, it's TURNING!" There's a sound like a great bell struck once, deep in the stone. The warmth in the walls becomes a roar of white light pouring down through the trapdoor. The great lamp has woken, a hard, clean white that has nothing of fire in it. It floods the stair, the doorway and the shingle. It is not hot. It feels like a hand set gently on your shoulder.

Outside, a low voice says something you only half catch: "Sixteen years, and still it burns for her." Sparrow's boots scrape on the stones, and then both sets of boots are running for the longboat. By the time you and Kit reach the door, the longboat is a dark smear pulling hard toward the Heron's Tithe. The grey cutter has her sail up. They are leaving, and they have left three dead hands behind. Your dagger lies in the doorway. In the clean light, you can see that the beam of the lamp reaches clear across the estuary to Saltmarsh.

Dunn's skiff hasn't gone far. He's bobbing off the point, staring at the light with his mouth open. Brann comes down the stair as fast as his old legs allow, weeping and laughing, his candle forgotten. "She said it would light," he keeps saying. "She said it would light."

It's half past seven. The grave is under the north wall. The cutter is making for open water, and the light cannot be put out while your lantern-foot stays in its socket. What does Wren do?

I retrieve my dagger from the doorway, wipe it clean, then walk around to the north wall with Brann and kneel at Elowen's grave. I lay the lamp-staff beside it, press my thumb to my forehead in the Lantern-Bearer's blessing, and say quietly, "I found it, Mother. I found the light."

After that I ask Brann to tell me everything Elowen said and did in her last days, and where the Grey Cloak fits into it.

A crooked-flame lantern is cut into it, and the letters *E.A.*. Her face looks straight up at the beacon. You lay the lamp-staff beside it, press your thumb to your forehead and say quietly, "I found it, Mother. I found the light." The wind is the only answer. Above you the lamp burns white, steady and warm as a hand.

When you ask, Brann sits on a stone and tells it all. He's slow, but he doesn't leave out what he remembers.

Elowen came to the spit alone in the autumn sixteen years ago, already fevered and thin as a lath. She said her daughter was "safe among people who will love her, far from the man who sells lanterns." "I thought him dead," he says, looking out across the water at the grey sail, now very small. "He had a way of looking at the lamp that I've never seen on a man since, as if it owed him money."

You now have a name for the Grey Cloak. Aldous. It is a little past eight. The lamp is lit and cannot be put out while your lantern-foot stays seated. The cutter is a speck on the grey water, three dead men lie on the shingle, and Saltmarsh is across the estuary. You've no spell slots left, and a lot of unanswered questions.

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Gullspit Light

Out of the story first, on both your questions.

On the name: I'll be straight with you. I picked "Aldous" for the Grey Cloak without checking it against Brother Osric's register, so it wasn't a planted clue. It does collide with Lord Edric's long-dead grandsire, and you're right to notice. I'll leave it open, as a possible lead and not a promise. Aldous Verrel would be far too old to be your Grey Cloak, so if there's a link, it's an alias or a family tie, and you'd find it by asking Lord Edric, Osric, or the Thornhallow records. It could also just be a common river-country name. Chase it if you like, and you'll learn whatever the world gives you.

On the lamp, here's my ruling, which I'll apply the same way every time. The great lamp burns only while the reliquary's lantern-foot is seated in its socket. If you take the foot, the lamp goes dark. If you put it back, it lights again. You'd need the foot to open Elowen's other hiding places, and the paper says it is the proof of your claim.

Now the story. Brann shakes his head slowly. "No surname, no house. Only 'Aldous', said the way she said it, like a thing she'd known a long time." He adds, with an effort, "The ship had a grey sail, much like that one. That's all."

Kit has finished laying out the dead. She stands up, brushing shingle off her knees, and looks at the sky, which has begun to cloud over from the west. "Weather," she says. Brann's squall is on its way.

So the lamp is lit and has to be a choice. You can leave the reliquary in the socket, so the light burns on and Brann keeps it, though you'd have no lantern-foot for any other doors. Or you can take the foot and let the lamp go dark again.

Dunn is ready to take the dead and the living back to Saltmarsh, though he mutters about the weather. What does Wren do?

"Elowen said to light it when the storm comes, and here comes the storm, so the foot stays where it is, Brann, and you keep the light through it." I squeeze his shoulder. "I'll be back for the reliquary in a day or two, once we've settled the arbiter and Corvin's statement. If the grey sail returns, ring the old bell and keep that door barred."

Then I turn to Kit and Dunn. "Load the dead hands, let's go before the squall is on us, and Dunn, I'll add two silver if you take us home dry."

You squeeze Brann's shoulder and tell him the foot stays. He nods, wiping his eyes, and swears the lamp will burn through the storm. If the grey sail comes back, he will ring the old bell and bar the door. You press two silver pieces into Dunn's palm. Then, with Kit, you load the dead onto the skiff as gently as the squall allows.

The squall arrives just as the skiff pulls clear. A wall of grey rain sweeps in off the estuary and the wind turns the water to choppy slate. Dunn's seamanship check is a 12 against a DC 12 that I set for the weather, so he scrapes through. Dunn grits his teeth, fights the tiller, and rides the lee of the mudflats instead of the open channel. You're soaked to the skin, Kit is grey in the face and holding the gunwale, and the three covered shapes slide against your boots. But you make the quay a little before ten, damp and shaken and still afloat.

Behind you the Gullspit light burns through the storm like a white thread, so steady that the quay-gulls wheel toward it. The whole waterfront has stopped to look. Dockhands stare out across the estuary, and someone is ringing a bell. A knot of Vantry guards is running down the quay. At their head is Pell, the halberdier who stood at the Salt Gull door, and behind him the arbiter in a cloak, her stylus still behind her ear.

You left your reliquary in the lamp's socket, so you don't carry it now. It is safe with Brann. The arbiter is looking at the dead men, then at you. Corvin's statement should be ready, and the lamp has told the whole town something has happened on the spit.

It is nearly ten. You have no spell slots, a hearing to give, and a long day's weariness behind you. What does Wren do?

I step onto the quay, wring out my cloak, and meet the arbiter's eyes. "Madam, three of the Heron's Tithe's hands lie dead in our skiff, killed when they attacked us at the Gullspit light, and their master is a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with a man named Sparrow. May I give you the full account, and read Corvin's statement, indoors and by a fire?"

Out of the story first: yes, there is word. The arbiter will tell you in the scene below. Corvin signed last night.

You wring out your cloak on the quay, meet the arbiter's eye and say it plainly. Three dead hands from the Heron's Tithe, a hooded man called Aldous, a man named Sparrow, and a request to give the full account by a fire. She doesn't hesitate. At the name *Aldous* her stylus stops, though she says nothing. "Indoors," she says. "Pell, the dead go to the dead-house, and nobody touches their pockets but me."

The elder's counting-room has a fire, a towel and hot cider with too much clove. You tell it in order, and Kit adds the dry parts. The arbiter listens without interrupting, then lays a folded sheet in front of you.

"Master Tallowmere signed before dusk," she says. "A clerk and my own guard took it down word for word, as you asked." She taps the page. "It names the last places he knew Elowen Ashgrove to have been, Ashby Weir and then a spit he never found. It names *H.* as a Master Hale, now held at Thornhallow. And it says Hale acted for a patron the prisoner knew only as *Aldous*." She looks up at you. "The patron paid for the whole trade in forged pedigrees. He wanted the ledger, and he wanted your mother's staff. Master Tallowmere says he never saw his face." She pauses. "He also says the man 'wears a dead man's name.'"

So the Aldous you heard about on the spit is the same man. Corvin's phrase fits the thing you asked me about, but it doesn't settle it. A dead man's name could mean a stolen alias, and the register Hale once tried to read could be where it came from.

The arbiter will keep the dead hands as witnesses and send a rider to Thornhallow with the name. She's ordered the harbour watch to seize the Heron's Tithe if she returns to Saltmarsh. The squall is still beating on the shutters. It is about eleven in the morning.

You have no spell slots left, you're still at exhaustion 1, and you haven't slept since dawn. Your reliquary is on the spit. What does Wren do?

I pocket a copy of Corvin's statement, thank the arbiter, and ask to have a rider carry word to Lord Edric: "Ask him whether any Verrel relative or old friend took the name Aldous, and have Brother Osric check the parish register for any Aldous baptised, buried, or struck out." Then Kit and I go to the Salt Gull, take a room, eat, and take a full long rest, because I'm out of spells and can barely see straight.

Here the rules bite, and I'd rather tell you straight. Your last long rest finished at 3:57 this morning, and only one long rest counts in any 24 hours. Another cannot finish until about 4 AM tomorrow. So you can't recover your spell slots or Bardic Inspiration yet. What you can have is a short rest, and you take it.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Corvin Tallowmere

The arbiter doesn't ask why. She looks at the rain on the shutters and at your face, then sends Pell down with you. Pell stays at the cellar door with his halberd grounded and his eyes on the ceiling, a man who is hearing nothing.

Corvin sits on a cot with a blanket over his knees. The black gloves are gone, and his hands look older without them. He sees the folded statement and smiles, rueful and tired. "You came back. I did wonder."

You read him his own line. He doesn't flinch.

"A dead man's name." He turns it over like a coin. "I heard it once, on a wet night in a roadhouse, when he'd had too much of the good wine and thought I was too far gone to listen. He said, 'It's only borrowed, Corvin. I'm wearing it until I've earned it back.' And later: the real Aldous was 'a Verrel by blood, and no friend to the Verrels' paper.' That's all he ever gave me. I think the man he is was never meant to have a name, and he's trying on one that has a claim attached." He spreads his hands. "Whether that makes him a bastard, a cousin, or a thief, I never learned. I swear it on the Lantern, whatever you think that's worth."

You ask about yourself, and the room gets quieter.

"No," he says. "It was never the whole of it." He looks at the wall for a while. "I didn't buy you, Wren. I told the caravan I did because it made a better tale. You were four, perhaps five. Elowen had left you at a roadside shrine-house on the lower Marrow, with a woman who took coin to keep you and ask nothing. I found it. I paid the woman more than Elowen had, and I took you." His voice stays level. "I told myself it was to keep Aldous from finding you, and that was partly true. The rest is that a child with Elowen's face, kept near the lantern-foot, was worth keeping. I won't dress that up. I raised you well enough, and I used you, and both are so."

You press for the name of the shrine-house and the woman. He shakes his head slowly. "Not from this cot. Get me out of this cellar into Dame Crowe's keeping, where the road is open to me and the man who smiles can't reach me, and I'll draw you the map myself." A thin, dry smile. "I know how that sounds. Your mother's staff is in your hands, and you've still not trusted me, which is the best thing I ever taught you."

You study him as he speaks. Your Insight check is a 13 (with disadvantage from exhaustion), and he doesn't give you anything to hold. Every word sounds like the truth, and it sounds the same way his best tales always did. You can't tell which parts are true and which are his craft.

It is a little after one. The storm is still grumbling overhead, Kit is asleep upstairs, and Pell is very carefully not listening. What does Wren do?

I stand, tuck the statement away, and look at him steadily. "You're not getting out of that cellar, Corvin, not by a bargain. Dame Crowe holds the assize at Marrowford at month's end, and I'll make sure you reach it alive and in one piece, because I want you to stand there and say all of it under oath, including how you came by me."

At the door I add, without turning, "And if you draw me that map from the cot, honestly and in writing, with the shrine-house's name and the woman's, I'll put in a word for you with Dame Crowe. Not before."

Corvin is quiet for a long moment. When he speaks, the warmth has gone out of his voice, and what's left is plainer.

"Alive, and in one piece, and under oath." He gives a short, dry laugh. "You'd have made a poor forger, Wren. You always told the truth in the wrong places." He lifts a hand toward Pell. "Guard. Paper and a pen, if the hall can spare them."

You don't turn around. Behind you the cot creaks as he settles. "In my own hand, then. The shrine-house, the woman, the year. If I lie, you'll know it when you've seen the place, and then you'll have the pleasure of being right." A pause. "Go and sleep, child. You look like a candle at the end of its wick."

Pell, who has heard nothing at all, unlocks the door for you. He murmurs that the paper will go down within the hour, and that he'll bring whatever Corvin writes to you at the Salt Gull himself and not through the clerk. "Seeing as the clerk was Hale's friend," he adds, to the ceiling.

It is half past one, and the storm is still wrestling the shutters. Up in the Salt Gull, Kit is sleeping. You've no slots and one Bardic Inspiration, and your long rest can't finish until about four tomorrow morning. Corvin's map, if it is one, will arrive by evening. What does Wren do?

You have 17 of 17 hit points, three 1st-level slots, three Bardic Inspirations and 71 gp. Do you stop at the spit first, or ride straight for Reedlow? What does Wren do?

Kit and I eat the porridge, load the saddlebags, and take the back road along the dike, with me riding Ember and watching the hedgerows for brown coats and grey cloaks as the morning warms.

You eat the porridge, load the saddlebags, and take the dike road with Ember's hooves soft in the wet clay. The country opens flat and silver on both sides, with reed-beds and drowned willows, and the sky is huge after the rain. You ride watchful, with your eyes on every hedge and gap. Your Perception check is an 8, and you find nothing worth a second look. There are no brown coats and no grey cloaks, only herons, a boy driving geese, and a cart that turns off at a farm.

You teach Kit the new verse as you go. She mouths it twice before she'll hum it, flat and surprisingly true, and by noon she's muttering the words to herself while she watches the hedgerows. "Not bad," you tell her. "Don't tell anyone," she says. It is the longest conversation she has offered in days.

You stop once to water the horses and eat bread and cheese in the lee of a dike-mill. The back road takes its time, winding around marsh and drainage ditches. The sun is low and gold when the land begins to rise toward a belt of alders and a flat brown stretch of river.

Reedlow Landing is a handful of low houses, a reed-thatched ferry shed, a stone jetty, and a flat-bottomed ferry tied against the current. A little way back from the water, on the old road, stands a small shrine-house of grey stone, plain as a cattle-shed. A tin lantern with a rush-wick hangs over its door, unlit. Two or three villagers eye you over their doors, and a woman sweeping a step stops to watch you come.

It is a little after five. The jetty and the ferry-shed are on your right, the shrine on the left, and the sun has about two hours left. You've three spell slots, three Bardic Inspirations, and Corvin's warning: *Say Elowen's name only after she has said yours.* What does Wren do?

I dismount a little way off, leave Kit holding the horses at the edge of the village, and walk up to the shrine-house door alone with my hands in view. I knock politely and tell the sweeping woman, who has been watching me, "Good evening, goodwife. I'm looking for Goodwife Annis Marl, or her kin, on a matter of the Lantern-Bearer's, and I'll say my own name first if she'll say hers."
